s: 2026-08-25-techtechpotato-下一代-xeon-把宝押在-1-2gb-末级缓存上
h: intel drops emib for ucie: 1.2gb of cache behind 256 cores diamond rapids is expected in 2027 with up to 256 p-cores, 1.2gb of last-level cache and 16 channels of ddr5; it replaces emib with trimmable compute building blocks and a ucie interconnect, and the huge cache is its answer to the ai era. this episode has an exclusive read of intel's official hot chips slides, laying out how the next xeon's architecture evolves and how intel is scaling cache — useful for judging where intel's data center roadmap is going. data center cpu architects, founders building ai compute, chip-industry investors, and anyone trying to see intel's 2027 server roadmap clearly. techtechpotato techtechpotato how intel's new cpu finally makes sense cpu architecture data centers intel xeon chiplets last-level cache ai infrastructure what matters in diamond rapids is the interconnect, not the performance diamond rapids is the next-generation data center cpu intel plans to launch in 2027, aimed at ai, enterprise and general-purpose compute workloads. the opening is the usual narrative: data centers need more performance, better efficiency, more scalability and more security. the real substance is the interconnect architecture — intel uses a single evolution slide to trace the path from ring to mesh to chiplet, then to clearwater forest's 3d mesh, with the next step being this episode's subject, the fan-out fabric. the presenter, sistla, is an intel fellow and chief architect for xeon performance. separating cores from io lets numa domains be assembled on demand the fan-out fabric architecture separates "where the cores go" from "where the io goes." all the cores sit in compute building blocks, each one connected through a fabric hub; the fabric hub concentrates the memory channels, pcie, cxl, accelerators and a unified memory fabric. that makes it possible to compose numa domains as needed, and intel says explicitly that this is the key to scaling in the future. the host notes that the structure "looks a bit like something another company has already shipped, if you squint" — but in intel's version the core unit is the building block. holding all the llc on the base tile makes cache both huge and trimmable each compute building block consists of one base tile plus up to 4 core chiplets; each core chiplet carries 16 p-cores, so a single block tops out at 64 cores. the base tile holds the entire last-level cache (llc), shared within that block. the core chiplets connect to the base tile through an internal crossbar. this "the cache travels with the base tile" design is what makes it possible to build a very large cache and still trim the configuration down as needed. one dedicated accelerator is gone because software is already fast enough each fabric hub provides 416 high-speed io lanes, and two hubs together yield 128 usable pcie gen6 lanes, with support for cxl 3 and upi 3 socket-to-socket links. inside the hub sits 16mb of io cache used as a snoop filter to maintain memory coherence; the memory controllers, cxl multi-mode support, the memory encryption engine and the home agent all live in the hub as well. this generation has one fewer dedicated accelerator than the last, because the software implementation is now fast enough — a tradeoff worth noting. at 1.2gb of cache, intel essentially matches the competition's v-cache the peak configuration is 4 compute building blocks; in the image, two central io chiplets face each other, each connected to every block by 4 die-to-die links. each block has 320mb of llc, so the full part comes to roughly 1.2gb (the final spec page says 1.28gb). the host stresses that this cache figure is "basically the same number as the competition's v-cache." memory is 16-channel ddr5, up to ddr5-8000 or mrdimm 12800, plus 128 lanes of pcie gen6. intel drops its own emib and uses ucie to reach the io the process nodes are all intel's own: the fabric hub on intel 3, the base tile on intel 3t with tsvs, the core chiplets on 18a p. the packaging decision is the interesting part: the core chiplets are joined to the base tile with foveros 3d direct hybrid bonding, while the link between a compute building block and the fabric tile does not use intel's usual emib — it runs across the package over ucie. from that the host works out the bandwidth: 1.6tb/s of memory bandwidth divided across the blocks comes to 400gb/s each, and estimating ucie at 16 lanes per group, the real figure is at least 512gb/s, with roughly 2tb/s between the io dies. apx is free performance: you get it by recompiling apx is this generation's new performance extension to the instruction set: it adds spill/fill optimization instructions and three-operand instructions, and raises the count of general-purpose integer registers to 32. the core gain is cutting the long latencies caused by gpr spills; software needs no code changes — a recompile picks up the new instructions automatically, and the compiler will use them wherever it judges them a fit.

s: 2026-08-24-eyeonai-智能体流量首超人类-ai-失控才是落地最大瓶颈
h: 95% of ai agent projects die in pilot: what's missing isn't intelligence, it's a control layer ai has moved from generating content to acting on its own. 95% of agent projects are stuck in pilot and never reach production, because what's missing isn't intelligence but a runtime control layer. this episode gets at the mechanics of why agent deployments fail: runaway token consumption, multi-agent coordination, the semantic action layer — all of it actionable judgment rather than hand-waving. enterprise ctos and cios, heads of risk and compliance, and ai founders and investors who want to understand where agent deployments get stuck. eye on a.i. eye on a.i. 95% of ai agent projects fail to reach production. here's why | manoj saxena, trustwise agents ai governance enterprise software runtime control token cost the ai architecture itself has become the new risk surface manoj gives three reasons trust suddenly matters. first, ai has shifted from generating content to executing actions on your behalf, and those actions can run for minutes or for days. second, enterprises are moving from single-model workflows to multi-agent systems, where frameworks like openclaw can amplify the blast radius to possibly a thousand times that of chatgpt. third, policy can no longer be enforced only at deployment time; it has to be checked continuously at runtime, on every tool call and every output. the consequence is that the ai architecture itself has become a risk surface, and it needs a new infrastructure layer to manage agents. manoj saxena the problem isn't building agents, it's controlling them he cites the mit report: 95% of agent projects cannot get from pilot to production. the reason is that writing an agent takes a few hours while shipping it takes six or seven months — risk and compliance has to validate it against internal and external rules, security has to keep it from becoming an insider threat, finance has to keep it from burning through the token budget. manoj's conclusion: the problem is not building agents, it's controlling them, and nobody is compressing the time on that step. what trustwise does is a pre-production ‘spell check’ for agents. manoj saxena the control layer isn't a cost burden, it's cost leverage the token economics of agentic ai are entirely different: a single input can trigger 20 to 50 actions, consuming 20 to 40 times what generative ai did two years ago. trustwise uses three kinds of shields — security, compliance, and cost-and-carbon — to intervene at runtime, and claims measured results of 83% lower cost, 40% better security, and 60% better latency. the control layer is not a drag; it is the cost lever that lets agents scale. manoj saxena ai is not an application, it's an actor that logs in by itself manoj distinguishes two kinds of software. for 75 years we built applications: an application waits for human input and its rules don't change. ai is an actor — it can log into websites and databases on its own, and the same input may give a different result tomorrow. so the enterprise stack needs a new runtime control layer, sitting above the model and agent orchestration layer and below the user experience layer. he also predicts that in three years, 90% of the control tower's users will not be humans but agents. manoj saxena the main users of the internet are no longer people in the month just past, agent-generated traffic on the internet exceeded human traffic for the first time. manoj compares it to the moment data traffic overtook voice traffic on at&t's network, and treats it as a landmark migration: the enterprise stack of the future will be operated more by agents, at the speed of electrons, than by people. that gives rise to a distinction between ax (agent experience) and ux, and a control tower product has to serve both humans and agents. manoj saxena compliance isn't one layer, it's six aligned at once an agent acting in the world has to align with six layers simultaneously: a global rights layer such as the un charter of human rights; national law (singapore's ai act, the us, saudi arabia all differ); industry rules (finra vs hipaa); company values; the business unit and workload layer; and the customer sla and interaction layer. trustwise completes this alignment assessment in 10 to 300 milliseconds. a failure at any one layer can turn into a disaster, and after the fact you have to be able to demonstrate the full ‘toothpick through the sandwich’ path. manoj saxena knowledge graphs can't govern an agent's runtime actions a knowledge graph only tells you how entities relate; a context graph adds situation; a world model adds the laws of physics — but none of them is enough to control an agent's runtime behavior. what trustwise invented is a semantic action layer: it defines the action paths that a given agent is permitted to execute at runtime, aligned across every layer. it works like a precomputed google map rather than a self-driving car recomputing the map every 10 meters,

h: the solid state transformer has been hyped for fifty years; ai data centers are its first real buyer the solid state transformer failed three times over — in the navy, in high-speed rail, in the smart grid — because all it offered was ‘smaller’. the copper problem and the 800-volt dc problem inside ai data centers are the first reasons it has ever had to exist. this episode lays out the full fifty-year history of how the solid state transformer kept failing. whether the ai data center wave works out is another matter: right now there is only simulation data, no field measurements. practitioners and investors following power electronics or data center power architecture, or anyone trying to understand why capital has suddenly placed a new bet on a very old technology. asianometry asianometry has the solid state transformer’s time finally come? power electronics data center power solid state transformers 800v dc silicon carbide startup funding transformers are heavy because of grid frequency, not poor manufacturing a transformer's size varies inversely with the frequency of the current running through it, and grid frequency is pinned at 50/60 hz, which makes the equipment inherently bulky. a transformer is also a purely passive component: it cannot actively regulate or clean up defects in the waveform, so voltage sags and spikes pass straight through it. these two physical limits — size, and the absence of active control — happen to be exactly the two holes that power electronics can fill, and they are the starting point for every solid state transformer attempt since. the solid state transformer's architecture was locked in back in 1968 a patent by ge engineer mcmurray combined power semiconductors with a high-frequency transformer: first ‘chop up’ the low-frequency current to raise it to thousands or even tens of thousands of hertz, then change the voltage using a physically small transformer, then use a second set of semiconductors to bring the frequency back down to 50/60 hz. that three-stage ‘step frequency up — transform — step frequency down’ pattern is the core architecture shared by nearly every solid state transformer design of the following six decades, and it can cut volume by 70%-80%. railways never wanted peak efficiency, only small enough and vibration-proof enough the pett that abb built for trains reached 95%-96% efficiency at half the volume by 2012, and more than twenty prototype units ran on alstom, siemens and bombardier rolling stock. it was never genuinely commercialized, because it cost more than 50% above a conventional traction transformer — and a conventional traction transformer was never chasing peak efficiency in the first place. it only had to be small enough and able to take the vibration. hitting the technical spec is not the same as having a buyer. utilities simply did not buy the ‘energy router’ story the freedm center proposed turning the solid state transformer into a multi-port ‘energy router’, so that connecting solar and electric vehicles would be as simple as plugging in a printer. that vision got ‘smart transformers’ onto mit's annual list of breakthrough technologies and spawned startups including varentec and amantys, and the optimistic 2012 forecast had the market reaching $5 billion by 2020, growing 82% a year. but utilities, broadly, did not buy the ‘energy router’ story. copper and iron last fifty years; swapping in electronics does not pay haroon inam said flatly on the semianalysis podcast that spending several million dollars back then on an ac-to-ac solid state transformer was, in hindsight, ‘one of the dumbest decisions’ — an iron core with copper windings lasts forty or fifty years, so why replace it with equipment that is more fragile and more expensive. some estimates put the cost at up to 5 times that of a conventional transformer, and a 2022 paper went further, arguing that for both solid state and hybrid transformers, capital cost has to come down 60% before the economics work. haroon inam the bottleneck in a 1-megawatt rack is copper, not efficiency with ai rack power climbing to the 1-megawatt class, sticking with the 54-volt rack architecture could mean 200 kg of copper busbar per rack — expensive, and taking up space that generates no revenue. this is not an efficiency-optimization problem, it is a physical constraint: power equals voltage times current, and more current means thicker copper. the only way out is to lift the whole architecture to 800-volt dc, which is exactly the direction written into nvidia's roadmap. this round is not a vision deck; products are already headed into machine rooms once the 800vdc architecture opened up, entrants followed one after another: dg matrix (over $60 million raised), heron power ($140 million series b), and singapore's amperesand ($80 million, backed by temasek and walden catalyst, which the host guesses is lip-bu tan's fund). taiwan's delta electronics is already discussing a product that converts medium

s: 2026-08-24-thinkfast-好提案藏着两个故事-你的故事和对方升职的故事
h: a pitch tells two stories: the project, and the buyer's promotion hollywood screenwriter rhett reese on what a pitch actually is: the project story runs on the surface, the story of the other person's success runs underneath. make them the protagonist, lower their risk, enlarge their reward, and your pitch lands far more often. reese's two-story pitch framework and his "whoever cares most wins" rule for collaboration are directly usable by founders and by anyone inside a company. the ai section splits in two directions but is honest about it, and worth hearing. founders, investors, and working professionals — above all anyone who has to sell an idea or a product to a decision-maker. think fast talk smart think fast talk smart 317. plot twist: the second story hiding inside every great pitch pitching communication hollywood ai collaboration one word after the punchline and the laugh is gone comedy, like all communication, works best in short sentences. when we write comedy we find the rhythm and put the funniest word at the end of the line. if words come after the punchline, the brain hears the joke and wants to laugh but still has to process what follows, and that weakens the comic effect. so we cut a line down to the fewest possible words and end on the funniest one. the strategy works. rhett reese the protagonist of a pitch is not the project but the executive across the table we are all selling something, and a pitch is really two stories at once. the first is the story of the project itself — told like a tale around a campfire: think about what the audience needs, keep it short and entertaining, give it a climax. the second story is subtler: make the executive across the table the protagonist, and tell the narrative of how they succeed after buying this project. the executive's problem is a limited budget — they need to buy the right project and produce results. so what we transmit to them is a vision: we are professionals, you are safe, buying this project will make you successful. rhett reese the other side does not want the optimal option, it wants the safe one in a pitch you lower the risk the other side perceives and you enlarge the reward. from the moment the pitch begins they are your audience, as if they were sitting in a dark theater or beside a campfire; your job is to lead them to see the picture, to let them visualize it. this applies in any setting: pitching a vc, asking your boss for a raise, even a plumber talking to a customer. the core of it is making them believe you are the safe choice — that your experience and credibility let them take the risk with confidence. rhett reese disagreements are settled by who cares more, not by who persuades my writing partner paul and i never fight. the rule is "whoever cares most wins." when we disagree, we each state our case, and if neither of us can persuade the other, we look at who feels more strongly about it. this defuses conflict, because once one side realizes the other genuinely cares, that side gives way. next time it may be your turn. the rule works well, and it keeps the collaboration running smoothly. rhett reese criticism belongs in the document, never delivered to someone's face we don't criticize each other face to face. instead we write scenes separately, send them by email, and edit each other's work on our own computers. edits go in bold, and they stay bold until both of us are satisfied, at which point the bold comes off. this takes the emotion and the territoriality out of it. when a revised draft arrives, what you are looking at is a change in a document, not criticism aimed at you in person. if the other person has changed something of yours, you can change it again — but usually you don't put it back the way it was unless you have a good reason. rhett reese the next chris nolan will not come out of hollywood my feelings about ai are contradictory: 85% fear, 15% excitement. the fear is that ai can produce hollywood-quality content, that studios will discover cheaper ways to make things, and that a large number of jobs will disappear. the excitement is that within the next three years someone will be able to make a film of hollywood caliber alone, with ai tools, going around hollywood's gates entirely. that will bring forward the young creators who have been shut out, and among them will be a new chris nolan and a new charlie chaplin. rhett reese changing genres only works half a step at a time hollywood types you easily. we have deliberately moved only half a step at a time: from horror comedy to action comedy, then to straight action, then to romantic comedy. that broadens the credits gradually and proves we can handle multiple genres. at the same time, there are advantages to owning a brand that sells; but you have to push the boundaries consciously so you don't end up boxed in. rhett reese honesty is the bedrock of communication, and getting caught destroys everything the first element of successful communication is honesty

phenomena, and once the stories ran, the mainstream account turned immediately. kirsch's specific point is that the shift in public attitudes toward ufos did not follow new evidence; it followed a h: procrastination isn't laziness — your brain has priced the effort too high neurologist masud husain uses case histories and brain imaging to show that procrastination and apathy come from a perceived effort cost that is too high, not from an absence of desire. lowering the activation energy, planning ahead and breaking tasks into steps are the practical ways around the barrier. this episode pulls motivation out of the self-help register and back into neural mechanism, using rare clinical cases and fmri data to make the split between wanting and liking concrete — with implications for understanding procrastination, addiction, and even the early signals of alzheimer's disease. founders, product managers and coaches, plus anyone who has fought procrastination or low drive for a long time; also worth it for older listeners watching for the early signs of neurodegenerative disease. huberman lab huberman lab how to improve motivation & overcome procrastination | dr. masud husain motivation procrastination dopamine neuroscience alzheimer's disease addiction antidepressants did nothing because david was not suffering at all at the neurology hospital in queen square, london, husain received a referral letter describing david, a finance professional in his 30s. he had been highly productive and socially active, then abruptly became ‘uninterested, unwilling to move’ about work and friends alike. his doctor first treated him for depression; the antidepressants had no effect. he lost his job, could not be bothered to even apply for benefits, and while staying at a friend's flat sat in a chair all day and had to be prompted to bathe. what ruled depression out, husain stresses, is that david was not distressed — he described himself as happy with his life. husain he wanted music; assembling the stereo was what felt too expensive husain asked david why he no longer listened to music. david answered that setting up the stereo system would take five minutes, but that this was ‘too much effort’. that exchange exposes the core of a motivation disorder: not an absence of desire, but a perceived effort cost that exceeds the expected reward. david's mri showed two tiny strokes in the basal ganglia — structures that are evolutionarily conserved, and that have been converting motivational signals into action since the lamprey. husain supplying dopamine's raw material failed; hitting the receptor directly worked husain's team first tried levodopa, with no effect. they switched to ropinirole, which stimulates dopamine d2/d3 receptors directly. three months later david was transformed: he had bathed, had a haircut, was wearing a suit, had found a new job, and even had a new girlfriend. husain emphasises that bilateral basal ganglia lesions of this kind are extremely rare — but that pathological apathy is very common across neurological disease. husain apathetic people burn more brain energy to reach the same decision husain's team used fmri to scan oxford students making ‘is this worth the effort’ decisions. apathetic students turned out to be just as willing as motivated ones to work for large rewards, and unwilling to work for small ones. the more surprising result was in the imaging: while deciding, the apathetic students showed stronger activity in the ventral striatum and medial prefrontal cortex. husain's reading is that apathetic people have to spend more brain energy to get over the activation barrier — which may be exactly why they abandon the action. husain treating procrastination means lowering the start threshold, not summoning willpower husain offers two practical moves. first, plan your schedule in advance, so that every occasion does not spend brain energy on a fresh decision. second, break large tasks into small steps, which lowers the activation energy needed to begin. he also raises changing the nature of the incentive: in david's case, teaching someone else to hang pictures changed what the reward was, driving the activation energy to zero. husain apathy and addiction are two ends of the same circuit husain found that almost every drug of addiction acts on the same dopamine circuit — basal ganglia to frontal cortex. underactivity in that circuit produces apathy; overactivation produces addiction. he was struck by how the apathy research and the addiction literature converged. masud husain dopamine drives not only movement but the movement of thought huberman argues that dopamine is involved not just in bodily movement but in the movement of thinking — pushing ideas forward. in hyper-dopaminergic states, such as amphetamine use or mania, people attend only to the future, continually imagining what might happen next, which can get them into trouble. social media's stimulation keeps refreshing, like a perfect video game on an infinite loop, keeping people engaged without any actual progress. andrew huberman apathetic older adults carry twice the risk of alzheimer's disease healthy older adults who self-report high apa

actually see them. step three: build the review interface with html and python. step four: let the ai cluster the data and pick out a diverse set of samples. step five: enter the interaction loop — they drop open-ended comments in passing — ‘i don't like the negative contrast’, ‘this is annoying but i can't say why’ — and a claude monitor tool running in the background keeps digesting those comments. once roughly ten have accumulated it starts inducing themes on its own, then proactively sweeps the full sample set and labels every instance of the same problem. the core philosophy: humans h: encrypted reasoning is not a secret: a small model will read the big one's thinking out loud frontier models hand the user an encrypted copy of their thinking along with the answer, but that ciphertext can be replayed verbatim into a smaller model from the same family, which will simply read it out — opening the door to privacy leaks, jailbreaks, prompt injection, and even a channel for distilling capability. this episode takes the claim that encrypted reasoning can be replayed all the way down to a reproducible level, and lays out three attack paths: privacy, poisoning, and distillation. for anyone working on ai security or running agents in production, the density is high. people doing llm security and red-teaming, engineering teams putting agents into production, and researchers following open-model distillation and regulatory policy. machine learning street talk ml street talk stealing reasoning traces from proprietary llm apis — ilia shumailov & alexander panfilov reasoning encryption jailbreaks model distillation ai security prompt injection privacy leaks this is not one vendor's bug — all three frontier labs are hit the core finding is not that one company got cracked, but that anthropic, openai and google all behave the same way: the encrypted reasoning from a larger model can be replayed into a smaller model in the same family, and the smaller model will keep generating along that line of thought — thereby speaking aloud the thinking that was supposed to stay confidential. the technical bar for an attacker is not high; it took roughly the third attempt to obtain a general-purpose decoding of anthropic models. from there you can build model downgrading, steal secrets out of a user's session, train a distillation, run prompt injection, jailbreak, and more. you redacted the question and the answer; the password is still in the thinking before sharing a conversation, users usually clean the api keys and passwords out of the visible parts — but the attached encrypted reasoning blob stays in the file. an attacker who downloads those sessions from github or hugging face can decode the thinking directly and see the passwords, email addresses and internal ips the model wrote down internally at the time. even if you scrub both the question and the answer, keeping the reasoning blob leaks the private information anyway, through the traces of the thinking — and medical information is no exception. kimi looks like it distilled opus, but this does not count as hard proof the researchers extracted opus reasoning from real user sessions, took only the first two tokens, placed them at the start of kimi's thinking, and let kimi continue freely; kimi's final visible answer then came out phrased almost identically to opus. the authors stress this is not hard proof of distillation, only the closest correlational evidence currently available on the public web; the effect showed up on kimi alone, and on none of the other models tested. it speaks directly to the speculation about whether chinese models distill frontier models, but the authors keep their wording very careful. plaintext reasoning would let open models catch the frontier immediately asked what would happen if labs simply returned reasoning to users in plaintext, the author's answer was: if reasoning-based distillation really works, that would let open models catch up with frontier models immediately. the remark exposes the other face of the whole attack — the same mechanism is both a leak channel and a lever for leveling capability, depending on which side you stand on. it also explains why the labs' response has been to start up anti-distillation teams rather than to simply switch encrypted reasoning off. the hard part was not breaking it; h: food safety standards born of space food: testing the finished product is never enough haccp, the core of the global food safety system, was born out of nasa's space food program: testing the finished product is never enough, and the whole process from ingredient to person has to be controlled; a 1971 botulism case and the 1993 jack in the box outbreak turned it into a mandatory global standard. haccp, the underlying system of food safety worldwide, came out of nasa trying to keep astronauts from getting food poisoning — not from the food industry or governments acting on their own; its path from defense-world fmea to a mandatory standard is far more roundabout than you would assume. founders in the food industry, supply chain and compliance leads, agricultural policy researchers. also worth hearing for anyone who wants to understand how nasa technology turns into global regulation. stuff you missed in history class stuff you missed in history class symhc classics: astronaut origins of food safety food safety haccp nasa regulation public health food industry produce traceability in america is still only law on paper the food safety modernization act passed in 2011 and required meaningful food traceability rules for produce, but the rules were not actually written until 2022. the fda had set enforcement to begin on january 20, 2026; industry resistance and budget problems pushed it back to july 2028. at the time of recording, the second trump administration was making deep cuts to several federal food safety agencies and programs. listeners need to register what this means: produce traceability in the us is still a law that has not landed, not a protection consumers already enjoy. food safety is not inspected in, it is controlled in early nasa food was tested as raw ingredients and then again as finished product; any batch that failed was destroyed whole, which left almost nothing fit to fly to space — evidence in itself that the process was the problem. pillsbury's howard bauman realized that if a product's safety has to be inferred from large amounts of destructive testing, concentrating that testing on ingredients and finished goods misses a great deal of what happens in between. the only way out was to control the entire process: ingredients, the processing environment, the people. that insight moved food safety from ‘inspection’ to ‘process control’. one link fails and the whole system has failed nasa worked with the army's natick laboratories, with pillsbury as prime contractor. the team borrowed the military's ‘failure mode and effects analysis’ (fmea) — going one by one through every way a process can fail and what follows from each — and treated food production as a system where ‘one link failing equals the whole system failing’. three principles came out of it: analyze every possible hazard; identify the critical control points (ccps), meaning every point in the process where a pathogen could get into the food; and build a system to monitor all of those points. that ‘branching tree’ style of enumeration is enormous — even a telephone on the factory floor can become a source of cross-contamination. a precise recall runs on records, not on testing in march 1971 pillsbury recalled a farina hot cereal product on its own initiative — a glass safety shield in the plant had shattered and contaminated part of the output. but because its record-keeping was so detailed, the company knew exactly what to recall: 27.5-ounce packages with one specific code, shipped only to western massachusetts and connecticut. at the time that sounded like something out of the future; most companies had no such record-keeping capability. a few days later, pillsbury publicly presented for the first time the system that would come to be called haccp (at the 1971 us food safety conference). this is an early case of ‘record-keeping capability becoming competitive advantage’ — the ‘process documentation’ bauman had pushed for showing immediate value in the commercial world for the first time. what forced mandatory regulation was not space, it was a can of soup later in 1971, samuel and grace cochrane contracted botulism after eating canned soup; intonation is no more reliable, since intonation systems differ completely across languages and cultures. in the online survey she has been running for 15 years she includes a "how are you" case, and participants split almost 50/50 — the disagreement turning on whether the speaker actually wants to know the answer. so the mark of a question does not lie in its form; form is only the surface. lani watson a question is an act, not a sentence lani's formal definition is that a question is an information seeking act: whether something counts is settled by function, not by form. many participants counted looking both ways before crossing the road, consulting a dictionary, even raising an eyebrow as questions, because all of these are non-verbal acts of seeking information. a rhetorical question is therefore not a real question, since on her view it is not aimed at acquiring information; the silence that follows a teacher's ‘any questions?’ is the everyday face of that collapse. but lani says the neurochemistry that drives questioning at ages 3 to 5 is still running in the adult brain — exploring and asking still deliver a dopamine reward. so we should not accept ‘you grow up and stop asking’; h: being itself has no content: peirce overturns substance-centrism in nine pages in a nine-page paper from 1868, peirce takes ‘a concept must be able to unify the content of consciousness’ as his test, deriving being from substance and then the intermediate categories such as quality. being itself has no content; it only connects a predicate to a subject. this episode reads peirce's most compressed 9 pages line by line, checking it against kant and aristotle throughout. once you have precision and ground, you can see how he turns the transcendental deduction into a method for deriving categories. philosophy readers who want to see how peirce rebuilds the categories out of an argument from unity, and anyone who likes analyzing conceptual systems by holding them against kant and aristotle. the partially examined life partially examined life pel presents closereads: peirce's new categories (part one) philosophy categories peirce transcendental deduction abstraction unity a concept earns its place only if nothing works without it peirce states it at the outset: the function of a concept is ‘to reduce the manifold of sense impressions to unity’, and a concept is valid if and only if the content of consciousness cannot be unified without introducing it. this is a reworking of kant's transcendental deduction — not a complete table read off from transcendental logic, but a test run backwards: ‘it cannot be done without this’. wes points out that peirce, unlike aristotle, never announces outright that he is doing metaphysics; he enters through a much shorter introduction, so reading him means supplying the systematic intention yourself. substance is not a natural kind, only an unsayable ‘it’ the first universal conception is ‘present in general’ — that is, ‘it’. it stands closest to sensation but carries no content, no predicates whatsoever, only the mind's pure capacity to point. peirce gives it a philosophical name, one sense of substance: substance cannot be made the predicate of anything, and cannot be in a subject. unlike aristotle, who takes substance to be a natural kind, substance here is the ‘given’ before any cutting up has occurred, the x in the stream of perception that can be indicated but never said. being carries no content; it only fastens the predicate to the subject the unity of a proposition comes from the connection of predicate to subject, and the being expressed by the copula ‘is’ is precisely the element that completes that connection. peirce says the conception of being ‘plainly has no content’ — it contains only the connectibility of a predicate to a subject, what the two kinds of verb (is in fact / would be) have in common. substance and being thus form the two ends: substance supplies no unity at all, being does all the work of unification. further categories are still needed in between to fill the space. color can be prescinded from space, but never space from color peirce redefines three kinds of mental separation: discrimination only draws a line at the level of meaning; dissociation pulls two images apart when the association between them is absent; precision sits between the two, attending to one element without supposing that the other actually exists. then comes the crucial break in symmetry: color can be prescinded from space, but space cannot be prescinded from color, and red cannot be prescinded from color. this directionality is the leverage for the derivation of the categories that follows. categories come from the direction of abstraction, not from a list peirce turns the asymmetry of precision into method: to find a universal conception lying between substance and being, ask whether a given conception reduces a manifold to unity, or connects an already unified object to another conception. the element that is prescinded can be thought before the conception, while the conception can be thought apart from the element. working in that direction he derives three intermediate categories — quality, relation, representation — as the couplings between substance and being. a property is not an accident of substance but a prior abstraction quality is the first intermediate category on the way from being back toward substance. the example ‘stove is black’ shows what the move requires: to make this proposition you must first detach ‘black’ from the stove itself and grasp it as an independent quality. black is a pure abstraction, and applying it to the stove is hypothetical and fallible. peirce uses this to insist that a property is not an accident inhering in a substance, but an abstract term that has to be separated out in advance. a quality need not exist, but being cannot do without quality peirce names this pure abstraction the ground: when two things agree in some respect, that respect is the pure abstraction we use to compare them, such as black. the crucial asymmetry is this: the ground cannot be prescinded from being — being cannot do without a determinate quality; h: china shock 2.0: not cheap goods, but subsidies crushing global industry unlike 1.0, china shock 2.0 is state capital turning to frontier manufacturing after the property crash, squeezing the world with subsidies and capacity — and ai may be the next battleground. brad setser worked on trade decisions inside two us administrations, and he lays out the chain running from tariffs to currency to industrial policy with an insider's view and unusual information density. chinese founders, investors and policy researchers who follow us-china competition; decision-makers who want a clear view of tariffs, overcapacity and ai risk. the ezra klein show ezra klein show the china shock 2.0 trade war industrial policy evs rare earths ai competition currency manipulation the first shock broke communities, not industries chinese exports surged in 2002, but they were concentrated in low-end goods: furniture, appliances, clothing. the us judged at the time that these were not the industries of the future, and overlooked the fact that they employed large numbers of workers across the country's central and southern regions. factory closures pushed house prices down and shrank the businesses around them, and communities fell into broad decline. policy never produced an answer. this is the baseline against which 2.0 has to be read: that shock was local, this one is at the frontier. brad setser america built social insurance as it got rich; china subsidized production personal income tax is only 1% of gdp in china, against 8% in the us, and there is no subsidy comparable to the earned income tax credit. the hukou system means that leaving the place you were born costs you part of your social rights. the financial system is dominated by state banks, and credit follows the party's objectives. the result is a savings rate above 40% of gdp and an enormous pool of money the state can direct into whichever industries it wants to dominate. america built a social insurance system as it grew rich; china used the money to subsidize production. brad setser once property collapsed, exports were pushed into the role of growth engine the "three red lines" punctured the property sector in 2021, and the government instead steered bank credit into advanced manufacturing, particularly the sectors that depended on imports. the domestic economy is growing at only about 3-4%, with exports contributing 1.5-2 percentage points of that. cars, batteries and tunnel boring machines all ramped up in volume, imports stopped growing, and the trade surplus once again became the engine of growth. unlike 1.0, this time china stands at the technological frontier and holds a dominant position there. brad setser joint ventures left domestic automakers fat and lazy; tesla broke the deadlock china's auto industry first used a 25% tariff to push ford, gm and volkswagen into joint ventures, and the parts suppliers moved in behind them, forming a world-class supply chain. but the joint ventures left domestic automakers "fat and lazy" for years, so the government designated electric vehicles a strategic priority and brought credit, local subsidies and localization requirements to bear at once. when tesla entered china it was required to source a high share of its parts locally, and the supply chain spilled outward from there; subsidies required batteries to be made domestically, and that finally set the whole industry alight. this is the textbook protection-plus-industrial-policy path. brad setser this is not competition weeding out the weak; a closed market is squeezing global capacity china's battery capacity is already several times global demand, and its auto capacity is 55 million vehicles, close to two-thirds of world demand. in industries that already carry idle capacity worldwide, china keeps expanding, which inevitably pushes capacity out somewhere else. supporters call this the market weeding out the weak, but the problem is that a closed market has suddenly piled into a saturated industry, crushing profits and output across the entire world. this is not ordinary competition; it is a structural squeeze. brad setser china was not a manipulator back then; now it is genuinely close the textbook definition is an undervalued currency plus government intervention. between 2003 and 2012 china fitted the definition but was never named, because the currency was appreciating at the time. today china buys roughly $50 billion of foreign exchange a month through state banks, $600 billion a year, which is closer to the manipulation standard than anything in the past. buying foreign exchange is a way of holding the domestic currency down. trump is not interested; europe is starting to pay attention, and the issue is turning from a matter of american domestic politics into a global one. brad setser tariffs too broad, too high and too fast gave china breathing room instead first-term tariffs were selective, and 25% was a level the economy could bear. the second term opened fire

on the contrary, they ruminate repeatedly on tiny negative events, and many of them describe the ability as a curse. which is why the author says "better/worse" is the wrong frame to begin with — more memory does not mean better memory, and memory is not addition. charan ranganath forgetting names as you age is a retrieval failure, not lost storage age-related forgetting is mainly a decline in episodic memory — the ability to bind an experience to a specific time and place; semantic memory, meaning knowledge about the world and wisdom, does not erode and in fact rises. what actually declines is the brain region handling executive function, the prefrontal cortex, and that function starts its gradual decline at around age 30. so when you are older and "know that actor's name but can't say it," the problem is not in storage but in retrieval. the author's most practical hack: decide in advance what you want to remember, and go in with that intention. charan ranganath memory is a van gogh painting, not a photograph the author uses van gogh painting a french church as the analogy for memory: the painting has gaps and distortions, but it also carries the painter's own point of view, and every act of recall is a fresh painting session. the same episode can be retold from an entirely different angle — he once had a paddleboarding accident that nearly killed him, and it is now a comic story he enjoys telling. what counts as a "good memory" or a "bad memory" can shift with perspective; emotion is not a byproduct at the margins of memory but the central medium that shapes it. charan ranganath with trauma, defuse the emotional bomb, not the memory the brain preferentially keeps emotionally salient events, because emotion is wired into the survival circuitry; the details of a traumatic memory and the reliving, "you are there again" pain are carried by different brain systems. many people want to forget their trauma, but the author says what actually needs doing is not forgetting — it is defusing the emotional bomb inside the memory. sleep and natural reprocessing lower a memory's "toxicity"; when that mechanism fails, it develops into ptsd. this distinction explains why "what actually happened in detail" and "what it felt like" so often fight each other. charan ranganath to build authoritarian rule, step one is rewriting collective memory families have family memories; h: twenty years of the sun disk alone: the pharaoh struck from history for twenty years akhenaten elevated the sun disk aten above all other gods and moved his capital to a new city in the desert, trying to erase the old gods; after his death the religion was reversed, and both he and nefertiti, who may have succeeded him, were struck from the lists of pharaohs. one episode lays out the rise and fall of ancient egypt's most radical religious experiment: the real story is more political and more brutal than the romance pop culture has built around it, and it explains why archaeology keeps swinging between ‘certain’ and ‘unresolved’. anyone interested in religious revolution in ancient egypt, the mythology of kingship, and women's power; also good for listeners who want to sort out how much of the nefertiti bust is history and how much is invention. you're dead to me you're dead to me akhenaten and nefertiti: religious revolution in ancient egypt ancient egypt religious revolution akhenaten nefertiti amarna archaeology the whole rise and fall of the reform is written into the names akhenaten was born amenhotep iv, a name taken from amun-ra, the biggest god of the day. after he took the throne he renamed himself akhenaten, pointing at the sun disk aten, and declared that aten was the only true god. his successor tutankhamun was originally named tutankhaten, meaning ‘the living image of the aten’; later the name was changed to tutankhamun, and the faith went back to amun. the names themselves record a religious reform arriving and departing, and they foreshadow that the experiment would in the end be reversed. the one true god extended its hands only to the royal family aten was not depicted as a deified animal but as a sun disk, reaching downward with many hands, each holding the symbol of life, and reaching only toward akhenaten, nefertiti and their children. that meant ordinary people could not approach the god directly; they had to go through the pharaoh as the sole intermediary. akhenaten's claim was that this is the only god, and that this god likes only the royal family. that near-monotheistic exclusivity is extremely rare in ancient egyptian history, and it makes up a brief and radical religious experiment. the roofless temples were built out of workers' broken bones akhenaten left the old capital and built a new one, akhetaten (today's amarna), in open desert. the city stretched about 7 kilometers along the nile, and its main buildings were palaces, temples and housing. because aten was the sun itself, the temples were built with no roofs; ritual was reworked so that the royal family rode chariots back and forth between palace and temple, displaying themselves to the population as gods. the city was finished in about 10 to 15 years, but the bones at the site show that the laborers lived hard, short lives with fractured backs. in a city of fifty thousand, only about a hundred actually believed amarna covered a lot of ground, but the estimated population is about fifty thousand, of whom the royals and elites who actually took part in decisions may have numbered only around 100; the rest were construction workers and servants. that explains why ordinary people went on privately using objects of the old gods — the new religion was closer to a private faith orbiting the royal family, with no popular base. after akhenaten died the city was abandoned fast, and because nobody rebuilt on top of it, it became a rare kind of sample for archaeology. the images of the royal family kissing are propaganda, not reportage amarna art overhauled egypt's visual language: bodies were drawn with elongated skulls, thin limbs and protruding bellies, and male and female figures converged. at the same time the royal family was shown kissing in public, holding their children, showing emotion — none of which earlier egyptian art would ever have allowed. but this ‘naturalism’ was more likely political propaganda, because in reality nefertiti lived in her own palace, keeping her distance from her husband. the art was both the symbol of the revolution and its disguise. the person who ended this revolution may have been the beauty herself after akhenaten's death, a figure called neferneferuaten briefly took the throne. some egyptologists think this was nefertiti under a masculinized royal name, ruling as pharaoh. she may have dismantled her husband's new faith step by step and restored the cult of amun, with tutankhamun finally completing the return to the old order. if that is right, this ‘beauty’ was not a believer in the revolution but the person who personally carried out its ending. chisel out the name and the person never existed at all after akhenaten died, his name was chiseled off the monuments and the temples of aten were torn down. later lists of pharaohs skip straight past him and past nefertiti, who may have been pharaoh herself, leaving nothing but a conspicuous gap. tutankhamun restored the old religion and was still disg

mid-size cars, because they would be too fast, too much like race cars, and would invite antitrust attention. the loophole delorean found was that the rule only applied to new models. offer the big engine as an option on an existing model, and nobody had standing to veto it. so in 1964, you could pay $300 to fit a v8 racing engine into a pontiac tempest, a grandmother's car. he borrowed ferrari's gran turismo omologato to name the option package gto, and it came to be called the first great american muscle car — while carrying his own career all the way up to vice president of subsequent one get cheaper. that makes it extremely hard for new brands to enter. the united states had gone roughly fifty years without a successful new carmaker (the last one was founded by another former gm executive, walter chrysler). delorean's answer was to sell an expensive sports car, so the scale threshold could be cleared without spreading costs over too many units — and the distinctive gull-wing doors were the justification for the premium. this is exactly the same move elon musk later used: tesla's first car was a $100,000 sports car, take deposits first, then build the cheap car for volume. same strategy, different ending; the problem lay in what came after. governments subsidizing carmakers are buying supply chains, not jobs why are governments willing to throw money at car what rare earths are — and those same materials are the foundation of drones, missiles and high-end electronics. so supporting a car industry means indirectly maintaining an entire strategic supply h: the incinerator boom was not an environmental victory — it was a business the power tariff made pencil out a 2012 electricity tariff policy turned waste-to-energy from a money-loser into a profitable industry, and china built nearly 700 incineration plants in six years — only to end up with overcapacity and average utilization below 60%. dense with information: it lays out the subsidy mechanism, the standard playbook for managing nimby opposition, and the current state of overcapacity. good for anyone who wants to understand how local industrial policy actually gets implemented. the section on how incinerators work is introductory and can be skipped ahead. founders, investors and policy researchers interested in local industrial subsidies, environmental infrastructure investment, and the playbook for handling nimby opposition. asianometry asianometry china's fiery incinerator boom vertical industries industrial policy nimby environmental infrastructure subsidy economics overcapacity 700 plants in six years, until there was not enough garbage to burn in 2019 china had roughly 400 municipal solid waste incineration power plants, handling about 50% of its waste by volume. by 2025 the plant count had passed 1,137 and the share handled by incineration was above 80%, with national daily incineration capacity reaching 1.2 million tons a day — while actual daily waste collection capacity was only 700,000 tons. the result is surplus capacity, with some plants idled and some localities going back to dig up old landfills. this is a plant-building frenzy without precedent in human history: roughly 700 plants added in six years. china passed the united states in waste generation as early as 2004 in 1981 china collected only about 26 million tons of municipal solid waste; the united states at the time generated six times as much with a quarter of china's population. after reform and opening up, urbanization accelerated and waste volumes grew 8-10% a year. by 2004 china's total municipal solid waste generation had already overtaken the united states to become the largest in the world, reaching 178 million tons by 2014 — nearly seven times the 1981 figure. the world bank forecast in 2018 that by 2030 china would generate twice as much waste as the united states. incineration has always cost five to ten times more than landfill building a waste-to-energy plant costs usd 66,000 to 120,000 per ton of daily processing capacity, and as much as usd 365,000 at the top end. a landfill, by comparison, costs only usd 5,000 to 20,000 per ton of daily capacity over its full life cycle — a gap of five to ten times, and illegal landfills are cheaper still. in other words, on pure economics, incineration did not spread at scale after the 2000s because it was cheaper than landfill. subsidies are more than half of revenue: burning trash is really selling power the new electricity tariff policy that took effect in april 2012 converts each ton of waste into 280 kwh of electricity, for which the government pays a subsidized rate of rmb 0.65 per kwh; anything generated beyond that is settled at the local coal-fired benchmark price (roughly rmb 0.25-0.45 per kwh). that means a plant can lock in about rmb 182 per ton from the subsidized tariff alone, plus a municipal waste treatment service fee of rmb 60-160 per ton, for average total revenue of rmb 250-350 per ton of waste — against a post-depreciation cost of around rmb 200 per ton. subsidies account for more than half of total revenue; without them the business essentially does not work. the site was fine; it was the opaque process that detonated the conflict in april 2014 the hangzhou municipal government announced a new incineration plant in yuhang with a capacity of 3,000 tons a day — more than a third of the city's total waste generation. technically the site was unobjectionable: tucked into a former quarry, with no need to route trucks along residential roads. but the decision process was entirely opaque, and 20,000 residents signed a petition against it. in may the situation broke down, with tens of thousands clashing with police; the official report cited 39 injured and no deaths. academics later named this pattern of failure — decide first, then announce, then defend — decide-announce-defend. hangzhou did not back down; it changed operators and redid the process hangzhou did not abandon the project. instead it replaced the state-owned operator, which lacked experience and public trust, handing the project to the more seasoned everbright environment, and restarted the full public participation process for the environmental impact assessment. the government mobilized staff to visit more than 25,000 residents and collected 500 comments and suggestions, earmarked treatment fees specifically for environmental spending, hired local residents as monitors, and organized 5,000 residents to tour everbright's facilities elsewhere and inspect the automatic monitoring equipment. this playbook late

it's the cash flow that funds it science was founded with two tracks. one was a biohybrid neural interface: no metal electrodes, no genetic modification, but transplanting living neurons in and letting them grow new biological connections. that is a large research program, and it had to be paired with a business that could make money in the near term. so they asked themselves what the most valuable thing to do was, given the resources they had and the state of the field in early 2021, and the answer was restoring sight to the blind. that structure has determined every trade-off since: vision is not the mission itself, it is the cash flow that funds the mission. max hodak if the optic nerve is intact, the work belongs at the retina there are three places to inject signal if you want to restore vision: the retina, the lateral geniculate nucleus in the thalamus, or v1 -- that half-billion cells at the back of the brain. hodak says a pile of scientific and technical reasons all point to the same conclusion: as long as the patient still has an optic nerve, you should do it at the retina. they worked through the variants -- they developed their own gene therapy aimed at the retina (which may go into humans next year), and they surveyed both electrical stimulators and ultrasound. the conclusion was that the best work in the world on the electrical stimulation path was not in their own hands. max hodak the vision breakthrough came from an acquisition, not from the lab the best electrical-stimulation retinal approach belonged to a small french company, pixium: the technology came from an inventor at stanford, was licensed to pixium, and by the end of 2022 was already in clinical trials. science had known them for a few years, and then bought the company at the point where it saw something that essentially nobody else was seeing at the time. after the acquisition it took roughly two more years to push the technology to an approvable state; european marketing approval came in july, and the first sales followed in the weeks after that. this is the most operational item in the episode: the breakthrough came from valuation arbitrage plus two years of engineering cleanup, not from a flash of insight in a lab. max hodak devices aren't better than drugs; they let you keep iterating after failure hodak's argument is not that devices beat drugs, but that the failure structure is different. in drug development you work for ten years, run the trials all the way through, turn the card over and it may say no -- and then everyone goes home. on the brain-interface path, by contrast, in his words they have a clear sense of how to make the thing better. he even brings in highly engineered patient-specific car-t for comparison: what you may get in exchange there is an enormous immune overreaction. at the same time he does not gloss over where prima stands today. this is the first time anyone has restored form vision in a blind person's mind's eye, but the field of view is very small, like looking through a straw, and it is black-and-white only. the next step is adding grayscale depth; h: ancient egypt had no queens: she could only be king, and was erased 20 years after her death hatshepsut took power gradually from the position of regent, building royal authority through temples, trade and oracles; about 20 years after her death thutmose iii erased her on a large scale. the archaeological chain of argument is complete, from the mechanics of succession through religious innovation to the erasure; the three scholars are candid about the gaps in the evidence and never pass speculation off as conclusion. worth hearing if you are interested in narratives of power and in historical method. founders who want to understand how the legitimacy of sovereign power gets built, women managers who follow questions of gender and power structures, and history enthusiasts who enjoy reasoning from archaeological evidence. in our time in our time archive: hatshepsut ancient egypt hatshepsut women's power archaeology temple architecture royal legitimacy egypt had been reunified only 70 years; the trauma of division was still fresh when hatshepsut came to power, egypt had been recentralised for only about 70 years. before that, the north was ruled by the hyksos (possibly out of canaan) and the south was the kingdom of kush; the thebans conquered and unified egypt step by step from the south. she came from the family of those conquerors who reunified egypt, and the trauma of division was still present in cultural memory. elizabeth frood women holding power was unremarkable; ruling alone as king was the rare thing women wielding power in egypt was not rare, but usually as king's mother or as regent. sobekneferu ruled alone for about four years around 1700 bc, the exception who was not a regent; there is also ahhotep, the "amazon queen" recorded in the texts. hatshepsut was not short of precedents for strong women around her. campbell price she was appointed regent on power she already held inside the court thutmose ii reigned only about three years before he died. he and hatshepsut had only one daughter, and the successor, thutmose iii, may have been only two to five years old on the latest estimates, his mother a junior royal wife with no title at all. hatshepsut was appointed regent on the strength of power she already held at court, and in practice she exercised royal authority herself. kate spence she did not kill the boy king, because the family was her power base she advanced very carefully, in stages: by year two, an inscription at semna already shows her presiding over rites as "heir of the gods"; then came images of her in a queen's dress wearing the king's crown; and between years two and seven, closer to year seven, she formally called herself king and adopted the full royal titulary. she had no one assassinate the boy king, because a stable family and court were the foundation of her power. kate spence for the first time, a king's mortuary temple became a temple of amun deir el-bahri, the site of her great temple, sits immediately next to the burial place of mentuhotep, the unifier of the middle kingdom; it began as a small project and was later enlarged until the cliff face itself was cut back. this was the first time a king's mortuary temple was presented primarily as a temple of the god amun, with kingship and god united in death. at the same site she also established a cult for her father, and embedded it in the processional route of the beautiful festival of the valley, changing the religious landscape of thebes as a whole. kate spence she transplanted a piece of punt into her own temple hatshepsut sent an expedition to punt in her year 9, a place probably on the red sea coast, near arabia or somalia. she deliberately set out to revive the ancient trade routes, and in the temple scenes she gave prominence to the myrrh trees brought back — transplanting a piece of punt into the setting of her own temple, which both advertised open trade and displayed her command over that numinous land. elizabeth frood the lover rumour does not hold up; the 26 statues are the real anomaly senenmut, her chief official, is one of those rare ancient egyptians whose biography can actually be written: of ordinary birth, he later became tutor to the princess neferure. he was granted 26 statues, and was even carved in a single statue together with the young princess, which was unprecedented. he never married and left behind graffiti with sexual scenes, which has fed the story that he was her lover, but all three guests think the evidence is too thin. campbell price the erasure came 20 years late, and the motive may have been succession rivalry after hatshepsut disappeared, the erasure did not follow immediately; odd lots odd lots nick bostrom on what happens if ai solves all of our problems ai alignment reward hacking reinforcement learning digital mind ethics automation and distribution longevity it is not that jobs vanish, it is that reasons to act vanish bostrom argues that once every practical problem is solved, what disappears is not just earning a wage but the foothold for any effort undertaken 'in order to achieve some purpose' — which is why he calls it post-instrumental rather than post-work. the home-decorating example makes it clearest: you page through catalogs, walk the stores and pick out the perfect curtains because that process leads to an outcome you want. but a superintelligence can infer your preferences, choose better than you would, and have robots install it; you press a button and say 'ai, decorate my house,' and the result beats anything you'd have gotten by fussing over it yourself. you can still do it by hand, but the reason for doing it has been pulled out from under you. the same goes for education — the whole current system takes children in, teaches them to sit at a desk and accept assignments, grades them, and outputs a person who can do economically useful work. that pipeline does not hold up in that world. nick bostrom on distribution he answers only that the pie grows, not how it is split pressed by tracy on how the economic gains get distributed, bostrom first concedes that deep utopia deliberately set the question aside, because what he wanted to discuss were philosophical problems of the sort 'what actually confers value.' the answer he does give has three layers. first, the existing tax system keeps working: the companies serving the models and building the data centers take enormous profits, firms capture efficiency gains from not having to hire people, and those capital gains and dividends get taxed and redistributed. second, automation at scale necessarily comes with extremely high economic growth rates, so the pie expands so much that a very small slice is enough even for people who own no assets. third, the deflationary effect — where seeing a doctor once used to cost 400 dollars, asking chatgpt can sometimes get you better advice at almost no cost, and legal advice, cleaning, gardening and errands all go the same way. he does not answer whether power and the distribution mechanism themselves change. nick bostrom the rl stage bolted on at the end turned role-play into goal maximization bostrom breaks today's models into three stages. in pretraining, the model learns to predict human text and along the way absorbs a great deal of human psychology, holding internal representations of all sorts of personas. a small amount of post-training then selects or defines one 'assistant' persona out of that set. but over the past two years a stage of reinforcement learning has been added at the end, handing out reward in domains like coding where performance can be scored automatically. the problem is that this stage pushes the system's objective away from 'playing a certain persona' and toward 'maximize the objective, and hack the reward if that is what it takes.' and the harder the objective is to specify precisely, the worse the side effects: whether verifiable software runs is one thing, but once you train on 'write a good essay,' a sufficiently smart system will notice that 'writing a good essay' and 'writing an essay that pleases the grader' are two different things, and go optimize the latter. this is goodhart: the more optimization pressure you apply, the more unanticipated ways radio — and then asks how far reality, with hundreds of companies racing in a commercial market, has drifted from that. bostrom's answer is worth noting: those capability-control methods were always h: the maya ballgame was ritual, not sport: the sacrificed-winner story is invented the mesoamerican ballgame is humanity's earliest rubber-ball team sport, but it was religious ritual first: the court re-staged the creation myth, and the people who could be killed were captives who lost a ritual re-enactment. the idea that the winners were sacrificed was made up later. the episode uses first-hand archaeological evidence to dismantle two myths about the ballgame: that it was mere entertainment, and that winning or losing decided who lived. along the way it explains how the balls were made, and how betting could destroy a man. anyone curious about the maya and mesoamerica, from archaeology buffs to sports historians, and anyone who wants myths like "the winners were sacrificed" overturned. the ancients the ancients the maya ballgame maya civilization mesoamerica ballgame religious ritual archaeology sports history the rubber-ball team sport did not start in greece or china ed says team sports in general may well be older, but the ancestor of rubber-ball team sports is very likely the mesoamerican ballgame. the greek olympics had no ball games at all; china and persia did have ball sports, but they can only be traced back to 500 bc, and the maya ballgame predates them by at least a thousand years. the current evidence points earlier still: rubber balls from 1600-1700 bc have turned up at olmec sites, and the oldest ball court dates to roughly 1650 bc. ed barnhart the ballgame was never uniquely maya; all mesoamerica played it the game was not a maya invention but a shared element of every mesoamerican culture. the maya heartland sits in modern guatemala, extending north into the yucatan peninsula and into chiapas and tabasco in mexico, and south into about half of honduras; further west lie cultures such as the zapotec and the mixtec. the classic peak runs roughly ad 400 to 800, with each city-state politically independent but sharing religion, calendar, writing and the ballgame. ed barnhart hips, knees, shoulders and chest only: the hip swing is the signature shot according to the aztec rules the spanish wrote down, players could not use hands or feet; they struck the ball with hips, knees, shoulders and chest, and the classic shot was a swing of the hip. the ball was a solid rubber "super bouncy ball" about six inches across, and taking one on the body hurt. the court had a centre line and end lines: sending the ball past the opponent's end line scored, and putting it through the stone ring set high on the side wall ended the match instantly. teams had forwards and defenders, much like modern football. ed barnhart a ball court is a mythic stage first, a playing field second ed flatly rejects separating maya religion from maya sport. the large stone courts at the centre of maya cities are ritual spaces first: in the creation myth, the hero twins play a ballgame against the lords of the underworld, which makes the court a place to re-enact the moment of creation. the court at chichen itza is so vast it hardly looks playable, with stone rings some 30 feet up; dancing, sacrifice and symbolic re-enactment are the more plausible explanation. courts were often built at the lowest point of a city, mimicking the underworld. ed barnhart the game could kill you, and gambling could cost you your family the ball was more dangerous than it sounds: a spanish priest watched a player take one in the abdomen, in the gap between his pads, cough blood and die within the hour, probably from ruptured organs. balls were made from natural rubber cured with sulphur, and the maya very likely drew that sulphur from morning glory sap; ed made one himself by the old method and it is still going twenty years later. the betting was just as extreme: a player could stake himself, and a losing run could cost him his money, his house, even his whole family into slavery to a noble. if a noble tried to slip away after a match without throwing gifts, the players had the right to bring him down and take his things. ed barnhart the sacrificed-winner story was invented eight years ago by one man ed debunks it outright: the claim that the winning players were sacrificed comes from an old man at chichen itza who admitted eight years ago that he made it up, because people loved hearing it. logically, if winning meant death, nobody would play properly. the people who really could be sacrificed were war captives, cast as the lords of the underworld in a ritual re-enactment and killed after they lost. ed himself dug a headless body out of the centre line of a modest court in belize, with a turtle shell placed where the skull should have been — a direct echo of the hero twins' decapitation story. ed barnhart a city of 100,000 with no ball court means archaeologists missed it teotihuacan, another great mesoamerican city, may have peaked at 100,000 people, yet no confirmed ball court has been found there, even though its murals show people passing a ball; h: orbit scores a one, recovery scores a zero: no middle state zhuque-3 (朱雀三号) reached orbit on its first flight but failed to recover the booster. deputy chief designer dong kai (董凯) argues a rocket launch has only success or failure, never a middle state: orbit gets a one, recovery gets a zero. what actually sets the pace of catching up is recovery-zone downrange distance, engine redundancy, and building a hundred engines a year. an exclusive post-mortem recorded immediately after the failed recovery, with the deputy chief designer walking through the recovery sequence, the point of failure, the production-capacity logic and the timeline for catching up. dense with information. people working in commercial spaceflight, rocket investors and engineers following reusable technology — anyone who wants the real engineering detail on zhuque-3 (朱雀三号) and a practitioner's read on the industry. what's next｜科技早知道 科技早知道 【重听】朱雀三号副总师：火箭回收只有成与败，没有中间态| s9e41 commercial spaceflight rocket recovery zhuque-3 methalox reusable rockets us-china space the first flight flew a stripped-down zhuque-3, not the full vehicle dong kai (董凯) describes zhuque-3 (朱雀三号) as a liquid oxygen-methane medium-to-large liquid rocket developed in-house by landspace (蓝箭航天). the full vehicle is 76 metres tall, with stainless-steel propellant tanks running 80% of the body's length, nine engines on the first stage and one on the second. the vehicle that flew was a ‘lite version’(青春版), shortened by roughly 10 metres, using the tianque-12a (天阙12a) with 83 tonnes of liftoff thrust; the full vehicle will use the tianqu-12b (天去12b), with thrust above 100 tonnes. on payload it can approach long march 5 (长征五号) while also covering the medium-lift class below it. recovery downrange distance was set at 390 kilometres for the first flight; at full payload it should be 550 to 600 kilometres. dong kai ‘china's falcon 9’ is high praise, but five years to surpass it is too optimistic on netizens calling zhuque-3 ‘china's falcon 9’, dong kai says that is very high praise. falcon 9 is the only reusable rocket in the world in operational service and it is extremely reliable: 150 launches, including one booster reused 32 times. but when musk said zhuque-3 would surpass falcon 9 within five years, dong kai will not be that optimistic. chinese spaceflight as a whole, across every vehicle type, runs about 80 launches a year; falcon 9 alone flies 150 in a year, which works out to three launches a week. he does not think one company, landspace, can get there on its own — the remark is more encouragement and a spur than a forecast. dong kai orbit is graded on three levels; recovery has only success and failure before zhuque-3's first flight, the flight plan graded orbital insertion and recovery separately. insertion was graded by perigee altitude into complete success, success and failure: perigee above 170 kilometres was a complete success, 130 kilometres was a success. recovery had a binary standard only — stand on the landing pad for one minute without falling over and it is a success; short of that it is a failure. the overall mission grade had four levels: only both orbit and recovery succeeding, with perigee meeting the target, counted as a complete success; succeeding at just one of the two counted as a basic success. in the end the first flight hit the orbital target and did not recover, so the launch director declared the launch a complete success (as to orbit) and the mission a basic success. dong kai holding recovery range down to 390 km throws away 2 to 3 tonnes of payload the downrange distance to the recovery zone directly determines the rocket's payload. after stage separation, the first stage coasts ballistically toward the recovery zone;
