h: 222-nanometre lamps kill pathogens and still sell a few hundred a year; the bottleneck isn't the technology far uvc uses 222-nanometre light to inactivate pathogens in the air while leaving the outer layer of human tissue unharmed; a south african tb trial is already seeing 90% suppression, yet the whole world buys only a few hundred units a year. the real bottleneck is how far the knowledge has spread. it lays out the safety mechanism, the cost structure, what scaling would take, and the failure modes; the middle-to-late stretch on building codes and the business case is especially worth a founder's time. founders working on respiratory disease prevention, people in construction and hvac, hospital operations staff, and parents who want their kids' schools to upgrade the air. complex systems complex systems the economics of putting germicidal light in every room, with misha gurevich and vivian belenky of aerolamp far uvc airborne disease public health startups building codes cost curves 222 nanometres is safe for humans because of a layer of dead skin far uvc in the 200-235 nanometre band, and 222 nanometres in particular, is absorbed by the dna, rna and essentially every protein in a pathogen, inactivating pathogens in the air at a rate equivalent to an extra 30-50 air changes per hour. the reason it is safe for people is mostly mechanical: human epidermis carries a layer of dead skin cells roughly 20 microns thick, packed with protein, which absorbs almost all of the far uvc. conventional uvc at 254/265 nanometres lacks that strong protein absorption, which is why exposure to it is not advisable. the eyes are protected by structures like the eyelids and lashes; they tolerate a lower dose than skin does, but the risk of long-term damage is very low. vivian the corner-mounted lamp is an existence proof, not the final form factor today's products are mostly mounted in a corner, because the beam angle is narrow and firing diagonally across the room maximises path length and average dose. the emitter puts out only about 100 milliwatts, and by the far side of the room the intensity has fallen close to zero; but the dose needed to kill pathogens is very small. misha calls the current lamp an existence proof: there is no insurmountable obstacle, technical or logistical, an ordinary person can buy one and install it, and in the future this becomes an ordinary ceiling fixture. the real obstacle is not cost or regulation but that too few people know this exists. misha elementary schools would gain most; workplaces will install it first vivian thinks the biggest benefit is probably in elementary and middle schools: ventilation is usually poor and children's immune systems are not yet mature. but parents hold safety to a high standard, so schools end up conservative, and workplaces, long-term care facilities and hospital waiting rooms will move first. the economics: one lamp covers about 250 square feet, an ordinary classroom needs 2-3, a university needs several hundred; a small building costs four to five figures for the whole thing, a large building runs into six figures; professional installation costs roughly as much as the lamp itself. patrick adds that waiting rooms have high turnover, so any single person's accumulated dose is low while total occupancy time is very high. vivian tb resists uv the most, and its transmission is already down ninety percent preliminary results from the south african tb ward trial already show 90% suppression of transmission: the guinea pigs were exposed to the patients only through the air. tuberculosis is not especially sensitive to far uvc, with roughly 10 times the resistance of influenza and coronaviruses, so the effect on common respiratory viruses may well be better. tb hotspots and nursing homes will be among the earliest sources of strong evidence. vivian says pandemic prevention is the most exciting case: the more transmissible the pathogen, the more leverage an environmental intervention has. old-style uvc once successfully controlled measles at an r0 of about 20, so pushing r from slightly above 1 to slightly below 1 is enough to avert a pandemic. vivian written into building codes, uvc becomes the cheapest path to compliance ashrae 241 is currently the only infection-prevention standard, but it has not been widely adopted by any authority having jurisdiction; once it makes it into building codes, uvc becomes the cheapest way to comply, and it enters the existing building stock on the ten-year renovation cycle. the alternatives all fall short: upgrading the hvac of an existing building is often impossible or extremely expensive; s: 2026-08-05-tyler-苏联把女人炼成超人-把男人宠成废物
h: the soviet union forged its women into supermen and spoiled its men into uselessness 27 million soviet citizens died in the second world war, and men became a scarce resource; the state used an abortion ban, rewards for children fathered outside marriage, and the decriminalization of domestic violence to forge its women into supermen and spoil its men into uselessness — an order that still underwrites putin's patriarchal mobilization. ioffe threads russian women and population politics through her own family history, and explains the roots of both putin's war propaganda and the decriminalization of domestic violence; her observation about flowers and gender signaling is a key that opens up russian society. investors watching russian market and political risk, analysts working on gender and population policy, and readers curious about how a postwar society remakes both sexes. conversations with tyler conversations with tyler julia ioffe on russian women, missing men, and the roots of autocracy russian society gender politics population policy feminist history putin politics the soviet female elite was made by tsarist radicalism, not by bolshevism tsarist law was harsh: without her husband's permission a woman could not do a great many things. but the same country had a radical tradition that produced women revolutionaries — sofia perovskaya, who assassinated alexander ii, was a woman, and there were so many women revolutionaries that the tsar had to build a separate women's prison. radical women were shut out of the universities, so those who could afford it went to switzerland to study medicine; the secret police then worried they were being radicalized abroad, and that fear is why russia opened women's medical institutes at home — to keep watch on them close by. after the 1917 revolution free higher education was opened to women and to jews, and two generations of julia's family benefited from it. but the root lies in the pre-revolutionary radical tradition. julia ioffe abortion became the only contraception soviet women actually had the bolsheviks legalized abortion in 1920 and followed with contraception in 1923, but contraceptive supplies were always short, so abortion became the only contraception soviet women actually had. by the end of her childbearing years, the average soviet woman had had between 3 and 12 abortions, and many had far more. stalin made abortion illegal again in 1936, but elites could still find a doctor while ordinary women went underground. ioffe quotes an old russian saying: the harshness of the law is diluted by the need to get around it. julia ioffe soviet population policy deliberately split childbearing from fatherhood the second world war cost the soviet union 27 million people, 20.1 million of them men. to ‘replace the dead’, stalin and khrushchev introduced the policy of 1944: divorce became extremely hard, which locked men into marriage, while at the same time men were encouraged to father children outside it. a child born out of wedlock could not have the father's name entered on the record and could not claim support from him; the state paid the mother monthly and handed out medals according to the number of children — and the medal scheme was copied directly from the nazis. the result was that a third of the postwar baby boom was born outside marriage, and an entire generation of children had a blank where the father belongs on the birth certificate. from then on childbearing was decoupled from fatherhood, the soviet single mother became a protected legal status, and men slowly became surplus at home. julia ioffe the belief that men don't grow on trees was manufactured by policy the sex imbalance hardened into a belief passed down the generations. ioffe says her grandmothers used to tell her that men don't grow on trees, and her mother warned her to secure a husband while she was still at university, because otherwise ‘all the good ones have been taken’. women were taught to maximize their own attractiveness, or another woman would lead their husband away — one russian sociologist scoffed: are men calves, that you can walk them on a rope over to a different barn? a whole postwar generation of women also never married at all, because there were no men to marry, and became pitied ‘old maids’. that trauma still distorts the russian marriage market today. julia ioffe the all-capable woman paid for it with 40 extra hours of housework a week the soviet union required women to work — a 1920 rule put all women into employment — and after the war, in order to raise the birth rate, it would not let them go home either, tying food rations and nursery places to women's jobs. so women had to absorb all of the housework and childcare on top of their work, and to make it ‘look effortless’. ioffe's grandmother was a chemical engineer who ran a water-treatment laboratory; explanation, lisa suggests helping the kid depersonalize it. picture a social group as a chemical compound, with each kid as an atom. when the compound is unstable, the members shore up their bonds to one another by expelling one atom — not because there is something wrong with you, but because this group needs its internal ties strengthened. the expelled kid becomes a ‘free-floating atom’: painful, but free. the metaphor hands parents a vocabulary for talking with their kid about being excluded. lisa what a parent most needs to give is not comfort but perspective when you are 15 and your friends abandon you, it genuinely feels like the world is ending. the parent has to walk a fine line: acknowledge that this is extremely painful, and at the same time state the long view with h: a $250,000 salary wasn't enough, so he extorted his own company ubiquiti's cloud team lead decided $250,000 a year was not enough, staged an intrusion into his own company and demanded 25 bitcoin — and was pinned down by a mac address logged by his own ubiquiti router. six years in prison. this is a complete specimen of an insider attack: privilege abuse, vpn cover, framing a colleague, and the forensic break that undid it all. every stage works as a corporate security teaching case. cloud infrastructure leads, corporate security teams, and anyone who holds the highest privileges at their company and thinks the pay is too low. darknet diaries darknet diaries 178: ubiquiti insider attack corporate extortion github vpn cloud security forensics the skills that got him hired were the tools of his crime nick had been working on video cloud services at aws's portland office, one mile from ubiquiti. in august 2018 he jumped to ubiquiti, leading the cloud division inside an 800-person team. even before hiring him, the company had noticed that his aws skills were an exact match for its own cloud needs. that job made him, several years later, head of the entire cloud team, holding top-level privileges over the aws environment, the private github repositories and slack — and that résumé is precisely the precondition for the insider attack that came later. $250,000 felt small because he was measuring himself against a billionaire nick earned $250,000 a year, and after a few years at ubiquiti he was promoted to head of the cloud team. but his pay stopped growing, and he felt his skills were rare and himself undervalued. he compared himself with ceo robert pera: the two were close in age, and pera was already one of the youngest billionaires in the world while nick was standing still. that psychological imbalance, combined with his habit of making a name for himself by discovering security problems, eventually led him to the idea of manufacturing a security incident that would give him a chance to shine. this was not an intrusion — it was access management failing outright nick used no backdoor and cracked nothing. at three in the morning he logged into aws with the same corporate credentials he used for work every day, found a key that unlocked the entire credential store, and logged out. two minutes later another account appeared, hidden behind a different ip, using exactly that key. he ran a single get-caller-identity command to confirm the identity, then sat back and watched for a week. the whole test proved only one thing: ubiquiti's access management violated the principle of least privilege — one employee could freely obtain the key to every system, and nobody would notice. what caught him was not technique but a 30-minute internet outage on december 21 he moved for real, using a shared high-privilege github account to clone private repositories over ssh. just as he was about to finish, his home internet went down. he spent 30 minutes on the phone with his isp, and although he had a vpn kill switch running, the github logs still recorded a portland residential ip — sitting right alongside his vpn ip. he later altered the aws log retention period and pinned 18 sessions on a devops colleague, without knowing that the real ip had already become the core evidence for his future conviction. his panic on the technical side mattered more to how the case turned out than his hacking skills did. a $2 million ransom cannot move a $23 billion company on the first morning of the new year, several ubiquiti executives received an anonymous extortion email: hand over 25 bitcoin (about $2 million at the time) or the stolen data would be published; pay another 25 bitcoin and the hacker would disclose the backdoors he had found. nick figured the company would pay, given the precedents of cwt paying $4.5 million and garmin possibly paying $10 million. but ubiquiti's market capitalization was over $23 billion, $2 million did not hurt enough, no ransomware had been installed in the systems, and the business had not stopped — so the company chose to ignore it. he also used keybase to show a senior employee the evidence sitting in a public folder, but keybase cooperated with law enforcement and deleted the data, and the extortion plan collapsed completely. a vpn can hide your ip, but it cannot hide your mac address forensic investigators found nothing at first in the company laptop and cameras nick had turned in. but when they examined the ubiquiti router in his home, they found that during the window of the attack a separate macbook had connected to the router over wi-fi and transferred an amount of traffic consistent with the volume of stolen data. a vpn operates at osi layer three; the mac address the router recorded comes from layer two, and a vpn cannot conceal it. that became the key pointing to a second computer. nick did not hand over the macbook right away — he reset it first — but the fbi arrived with a search warrant on march

run inference with the real weights to collect hidden states and retrain the speculator; then add runtime support for the new architecture (glm-5.2's dsa sparse attention is borrowed from deepseek). because the model api side is zero data retention, they do not know what the actual traffic is and can only approximate it with public datasets — ‘coding and agents are the mainstream’ — to train a general-purpose speculator. even when k2.5 to k2.6 is nothing more than continued post-training, there is no dodging this pipeline. philip vision can be transplanted, and the backbone loses nothing at all open models can take organ transplants. haley on the team grafted kimi's vision encoder onto glm-5.2: both the encoder and the backbone weights stay frozen, and only the projector in between — a few million parameters — gets trained, because touching the backbone weights risks the model getting dumber at something else. the first version was trained only on ‘describe this image’ data and never learned properly; after switching to a set of discriminative questions per image (is there a bird in the picture, is there a scientist), grokking appeared. the result is 56% on mmlu pro — not frontier — but when there is no image input the encoder is skipped outright, so the original glm-5.2 quality loses nothing at all. what you end up with is a model stitched together from kimi's eyes, glm's weights and deepseek's attention. philip mode collapse is not the weights' fault, it is the cluster's glm-5.2 and dsv 4 have both shown mode collapse — emitting the same token over and over, most often s — and it happens even at temperature 0.9. their read is that this is not a weights problem. take the same weights to a different inference engine (sglang to vllm), or merge in the changes from nvidia's new tensorrt-llm image, and the problem disappears. a more extreme case: the same model would collapse on one cluster and not on another, because on the first the interconnect carrying kv cache transfers between nodes was slower, which exposed a race condition in a kernel that was missing a synchronization barrier — the eventual fix was to host it on a different cluster. there is also a backstop in production: if the same token appears more than four times in a row, cut it off and rerun — but you have to exclude special characters like table separator lines. ali pick the right layers and 20% more quantization comes out more faithful the industry default is ‘the more you quantize, the more you lose’; h: palestine is not a national cause but a self-reproducing symbol-extraction machine stop treating palestine as a single national cause — inside the middle east's power structure it is a machine that converts suffering into an asset for every party involved: no centre, no king that could be killed, and no way out except clarity at the personal level. taking the palestine question apart as a rent-seeking system, in the language of political economy, is both rare and dense. the second half turns to religious philosophy and gets speculative; readers who only want the mechanism can skip it. middle east researchers, investors in international aid and education, university policymakers, and anyone trying to work out how ideology gets its value amplified by capital and by regimes. econtalk econtalk the political economy of palestine (with hussein aboubakr mansour) middle east politics rent-seeking ideology qatar palestine victimhood narrative the same victimhood is cashed in at once by mutually hostile camps the host asks why palestine is able to drive narratives that are incompatible with one another. mansour's answer is a political economy with no national centre in it: the conflict contains an ‘autopoietic symbolic convertibility machine’, and the same unit of victimhood can be converted simultaneously by left-wing, right-wing, religious and nationalist ideological markets into value that reinforces itself across all of them. he stresses that this is a property of ‘today’, not a historical fate: the machine has been running in the middle east since 1948, and only in the past decade has it finished globalising. to understand it, the question to ask is not which side is more just, but how the structure recycles every participant's moral investment back into the same loop. hussein aboubakr mansour every problem in the arab world eventually runs into israel mansour says that when he was growing up in egypt, anti-israel feeling was close to the bedrock of identity. its real power was not the slogans but an attribution chain that can be reused without limit: the arab world lacks democracy because the united states suppresses democracy in order to protect israel; economic failure is attributed to sadat's open-door policy; the open-door policy came out of the camp david accords; and the camp david accords are understood as an arrangement to guarantee israel's security. follow any social or economic problem to the end of that causal chain and you arrive at the same enemy. this intellectual structure hands every discussion a ready-made recycling route, and it explains why even concrete development problems end up back at the palestinian symbol. hussein aboubakr mansour anti-israel feeling has to run hot, but never too hot arab regimes face a thermostat problem: anti-israel feeling has to run hot enough to divert the public from questions about the domestic political system, but must never run so hot that the opposition — islamist movements above all — can adopt a more strident position and bite back at the regime for ‘colluding with israel’. so each regime keeps several temperature dials in hand and adjusts them as internal risk and the regional game require. that also turns the issue into an instrument of state-to-state play: qatar can have al jazeera stoke palestinian feeling inside other countries to manufacture instability, while iran tries to occupy the position of ‘guardian of the palestinian symbol’, so that the victimhood narrative becomes its own source of premium within the middle eastern order. hussein aboubakr mansour saudi arabia insists on palestinian statehood precisely because it knows it is impossible by 2025 official saudi language had hardened into ‘a palestinian state is the region's only way out’, but mansour says the saudi elite knows perfectly well that the goal cannot be achieved — deliberately demanding the impossible is exactly the bargaining chip in the new game. earlier, the uae had tried to reverse the rules, turning ‘recognition of israel’ into an asset for arab states dealing with the west, and saudi arabia followed that direction for a time. after october 7, with the iranian threat weakened and the palestinian symbol appreciating globally, saudi arabia recalculated: returning to the old confrontation game lets it suppress the uae's positioning and maintain a military balance against israel at the same time. what decides the public stance is not justice but each state's relative price in this extraction market. hussein aboubakr mansour what qatar is buying is not reputation, it is proxy power mansour treats qatar as the most serious case inside the american higher education system: a small state of only three hundred thousand people, with no military weight, has put roughly $20 billion into us universities. what the money buys is not just reputation but proxy power — us central command is based on qatari soil, qatar has become washington's main interlocutor with tehran, and it freed hostages

h: tungsten's price spike is a hundred-year war prediction market: china cuts supply and it goes up tenfold tungsten's supply-and-demand cycle behaves like a war prediction market: prices spike before wars and collapse after them. china controls eighty percent of supply, and the west could restart old mines for only tens of millions of dollars — but with no futures market, the projects are hard to finance. through the story of one hundred-year-old tasmanian tungsten mine coming back into production, this episode works through the pricing dilemma of strategic minerals and the geopolitics around them. useful for understanding critical-minerals investing and supply-chain risk. investors watching critical-minerals supply chains, mining analysts, geopolitics researchers, and founders who want to understand the pricing dilemma of strategic minerals. odd lots odd lots the tungsten market is warning of an upcoming war tungsten critical minerals geopolitics supply chains mining investment war economy every restart of a tungsten mine lines up with a war david fickling argues that tungsten's history reads like a war prediction market that has been running for a century. mine owners talk to tungsten traders, traders talk to defence manufacturers, and the defence firms are the first to place orders when war is approaching. the dolphin mine he visited opened during world war i and closed after it, reopened before world war ii, was rescued by the korean war, was abandoned after the cold war, and is now restarting again because of war risk. that repeating cycle shows how tightly tungsten demand tracks expectations of war — and how thoroughly it is ignored in peacetime. david fickling armour-piercing rounds rely on tungsten's density, not its hardness tungsten's military value comes from its density and melting point: as dense as gold, with a melting point above three thousand degrees celsius, three times that of magma. armour-piercing rounds use it to hold their shape as s: 2026-07-31-cautionary-约克郡女巫罪案-骗局的核心是权力欲
h: dissected and displayed after hanging: what she threatened was order, not money mary bateman, an 18th-century fraudster, worked through fortune-telling and a poisoned pie — not for the money, but for the pleasure of control. her cons landed precisely on what people wanted to believe, and after her death her body was still put on display, exposing how much a society feared anyone who upended its order. rich in historical detail, and the second half is especially strong where it moves from the individual case up to the mechanics of modern scams; if you only want the crime story, the middle stretch drags a little. anyone interested in the psychology of scams, historical crime and how trust works; product and marketing people can use it to recognise the techniques used to manipulate users. cautionary tales with tim harford cautionary tales arsenic and lace: the trial of the yorkshire witch - with maddy pelling scams psychological manipulation 18th century historical crime fraud defence desire for power once the con artist blends into the crowd, magic's tacit bargain collapses in the 1740s, a magician announced he would climb inside a bottle on stage at the haymarket theatre in london. the audience paid for tickets, expecting to suspend disbelief and enjoy an ingenious deception. but the performer never appeared, the crowd rioted at having been made fools of, and soldiers were eventually called in to put it down. maddie points out that up to then there had been a tacit bargain between magic acts and their audiences: what happened on stage was a safe illusion, and the audience played along knowing full well it was fake. the moment the trickster broke that contract and melted into the crowd — becoming any stranger at all — every kind of trust stopped working. the episode reads as a metaphor for the era: all the settled rules were being rewritten. maddy pelling she was not short of money; what the con bought her was private control after a mill fire, a pregnant mary went door to door collecting bandages for the hospital, then turned around and sold every one of them. she was not short of money: her husband john was a wheelwright with a respectable income and a place in the militia. maddie stresses that mary's behaviour came out of a craving for private control, not an economic motive. she was skilled at using her pregnancy to win trust, at reading other people's fears, at offering comfort that seemed uncannily precise — and then destroying them completely. that pattern of manipulation runs through her whole life, and foreshadows the far graver crimes that followed. maddy pelling the con does not end in money; it ends in a pie laced with arsenic rebecca perigo was chronically unwell, and mary claimed the cure required spells worked through an intermediary, a miss blythe, luring the couple into handing over nearly everything they owned — a new bed, hams, gold coins. when william grew suspicious, mary's final instruction was that they eat a pie with a powder mixed into it, then take honey to cover the bitterness. rebecca ate a few mouthfuls, then was rolling on the floor vomiting, and died in agony days later; william survived because he took only one bite. he set a trap to lure mary in, and she was carrying a small bottle of arsenic on her person, with several of her victims' possessions found in her house. at that point the con had escalated from psychological manipulation to lethal poisoning. maddy pelling the letter she told him to burn became the evidence that hanged her at trial william produced the letters mary had written him — she had told him to burn them after reading, but he kept them, and they became the strongest physical evidence against her. several doctors examined the remains of the pie and the vomit; one of them even had a heart attack in the courtroom. sentenced to hang, mary tried ‘pleading the belly’, and the judge closed the court so that women present could examine her; the conclusion was that she was not pregnant. a prison keeper recalled her nursing her baby one last time, handing the child to her husband, and walking to the gallows. mary was still lying up to the moment she died, but the chain of evidence could no longer be overturned. maddy pelling hanging her was not enough; she had to be boiled into an exhibit after mary was hanged, her body was taken back to the anatomy school in leeds, where the anatomist william hay charged admission for three days, took the corpse apart in front of the crowd, and held up her womb to announce there was no baby in it; spectators joked that the heart wasn't black enough. her remains were boiled and then exhibited, and her bones stayed museum exhibits until 2015. visitors queued to touch the bones, afraid she would come back for revenge. maddie argues that this extreme treatment shows she had shaken the hierarchical order of an emerging capitalism, and so had to be erased entirely, not merely executed. maddy pelling she made a living by defying the system

but using the methods of physics to structure research first, then training a meta model to predict training curves, so that ai eventually discovers the next generation of architectures on its own. a inheritance in order to succeed, which is why the demands it places on architecture are low. other modalities, vision above all, have not been compressed in the same way, so a world model needs an architecture designed to learn abstract representations. that is exactly why model design has become important again in the post-llm era. liu ziming most afai work runs neural to neural and never closes the loop liu sums up his own research as a single thread: grafting the neural and the symbolic worlds together. ai for science uses neural methods to capture symbolic scientific laws; science of ai runs the other way, using symbolic and scientific methods to understand and improve the ai black box. what most people call afai, he points out, mostly goes from neural to neural and never closes the loop back to the symbolic part. his afai is ‘ai for physics of ai’: using ai to accelerate the understanding of ai itself, and then using that understanding to design better models. liu ziming top talent would rather go solo than be foot soldiers at big labs liu's view is that the reason a wave of neo labs has appeared in china and the us at the same time comes down to a change in temperature emerges from atoms. this is not just philosophical sport: people who read that ‘free will is an illusion’ become more willing to cheat and less willing to help others. it bears directly on cites a body of psychology experiments: subjects are given something to read along the lines of ‘science has proven free will is an illusion’, and then their behaviour is observed. people turn out to of responsibility and their moral behaviour. merrill horn people are trains stuck on rails, unable to escape the laws of physics the usual definition of free will is this: when choosing between chocolate and caramel, it is ‘i’ who decides, and it is not a roll of the dice. but classical physics describes a clockwork universe: a ball rolls down a hill because of gravity, and every event is determined by prior causes. a human body is likewise a collection of molecules, and in principle the next step could be predicted from the laws of physics and biology. john dylan haynes, at the charité in berlin, uses the image of railway tracks: a person is like a train stuck on rails, unable to leave the path that natural law has laid out. merrill horn the brain settles it seven seconds in the scalp eeg. john replicated and extended this with fmri: 14 subjects freely chose to press a left or right button, and the brain signal appeared a full 7 seconds before people reported making the decision. wendy times out 7 seconds live on air to show how long that is — your brain may have prepared the decision well in advance, with consciousness riding along as a passenger who finds out afterwards. merrill horn sixty percent accuracy cannot carry the claim that the decision is already made john used machine learning on the brain signals to see whether left or right could be predicted before the subject was aware of choosing. accuracy came out around 60% — better than a coin flip's 50%, but far from perfect. merrill does not buy 60%; another group, using a different technique, pushed the prediction rate to 80% in the instant before the decision. this research became ammunition in the argument: john's paper has been cited by other papers nearly 3,000 times. for those on the h: tens of thousands of earthworks under the amazon, and a civilization of perhaps three million using lidar to see through the rainforest canopy, archaeologists have found tens of thousands of earthworks in the southwestern amazon, spread across more than 180,000 square kilometres, with a peak population that may have reached 3 million. the first segment is an archaeological finding that resets what we thought about the region, backed by hard numbers; the last two segments are lighter science chat. medium information density, fine for a commute, and the amazon part is worth writing down. archaeology enthusiasts and environmental professionals who follow pre-columbian amazonia, and also biology students interested in cephalopod evolution. nature podcast nature podcast earthworks spotted in the amazon hint at huge ancient civilization amazon archaeology lidar cephalopod fossils fungal textiles ancient civilizations science findings there is an order of magnitude more earthwork buried under the amazon than anyone guessed marti pärssinen's team used airborne lidar to survey roughly 4,500 square kilometres of acre and amazonas states, and found around 430 earthworks beneath dense canopy, more than 40 of them never seen before. extrapolating from that plus earlier data, the team estimates the region holds 24,000 to 30,000 earthworks in total — an order of magnitude more than the 2,000-3,000 marti himself had previously guessed. most of the earthworks are geometric geoglyphs and roads, built between roughly 600 bc and ad 850. marti pärssinen satellites only see the cleared land; only lasers see beneath the forest the earthworks went undetected for so long because more than half of acre state and most of amazonas state are still forest-covered, and satellite imagery can only show the deforested areas. a lidar system fires rapid laser pulses at the ground; some of the beams slip through gaps in the canopy, reach the ground and reflect back, which builds a three-dimensional map of the terrain under the trees. within the area mapped on these flights, the team found not only earthworks hidden by trees but also grassland structures that satellite images had missed — probably because the grass was too dense for them to show at the surface. pre-colonial amazonia was not wilderness, it was home to three million people extrapolating from the new findings, the team puts the total area of the ari civilization at more than 180,000 square kilometres, over three times previous estimates. working back from the labour needed to maintain the earthworks, the local population at its height in ad 100-300 may have been between 1.25 million and 3 million. marti concedes that these extrapolations are contested, and says a genuinely accurate answer would need more lidar flights, which are expensive; he believes the real number is about ten times more than he had previously imagined. this unsettles the old narrative that pre-colonial amazonia was wilderness — humans had already urbanised there and altered the soils and the biodiversity. marti pärssinen clothing that heals itself will also rot in the ground chinese researchers grew the mycelium of the cordyceps militaris fungus into a dense network, then chemically treated it to make it flexible, and were also able to dye it in natural pale blues, reds, oranges and purples by adding pigment-producing yeasts. this living textile is self-cleaning, and when torn it will grow back together with nothing more than added nutrients and fresh mycelium. discarded samples decomposed in soil in 41 days. but biodegradability brings its own trouble: under heat and humidity the material stretches and deforms easily, which is the main obstacle to commercialising it for clothing and packaging. small bubbles are louder than big ones, and the sound reveals their size french physicists wanted to work out what determines how loud a bubble is when it enters water. they made bubbles two ways: squirted directly out of an underwater nozzle, or formed when a droplet hits the water surface and makes a crater that closes and traps a bubble. the results showed that the small bubbles from the droplet method were often louder than the larger bubbles the nozzle produced; and a given bubble is also louder when contracting than when growing. the work could be used to infer bubble size and state from sound, with potential uses including monitoring underwater gas leaks. cephalopods learned to adjust buoyancy and leave the seafloor almost as soon as they appeared palaeontologists have reported a set of small fossils roughly 515 million to 521 million years old, with shells about 4.5 millimetres long, internally divided into chambers, and preserving the soft-tissue siphuncle — the structure modern cephalopods use to pump gas in and water out of the chambers to control buoyancy. the oldest cephalopod fossils previously known were around 490-495 million years old, while cephalopods split from the other molluscan branches around 525

goal suits tasks that can make sustained, verifiable progress; most tasks are neither. the slider is designed to project a multi-dimensional space onto one dimension by force: speed and efficiency at one end, quality and thoroughness at the other. after launch they also changed ultra so you have to turn it on manually in advanced settings, because it burns through usage limits faster. akshay nathan sites are replacing the deck-plus-spreadsheet most of the discussion around sites focuses on their prototyping side; inference no longer depends on beam search, and that continuing to maintain it would only pile on complexity the project could not sustain. that willingness to cut is what lets an open-source project troubles’: training outfits file junk prs to pad their students' résumés, and bot accounts have shown up that submit 20 prs in 10 minutes, breaking the assumption that everyone in the community is h: ai won't break sap, but it will break per-seat pricing ai will not flatten what enterprise software has accumulated, but it will break the per-seat pricing model. sap's defense is not training its own foundation model — it is open partnership plus business understanding, and the real battlefield is the last mile: process, data and organizational inertia. a rare view from an executive inside a legacy enterprise-software giant, using specific numbers and cases to puncture the ‘the model is the product’ illusion, and explaining why 28% have tried ai while only 3% see a return. enterprise-software founders, investors, technology leaders at companies expanding abroad, and engineers trying to work out whether fde is a good career direction. 晚点聊 latetalk 晚点聊 174: ai冲击企业软件巨头？与sap原欣聊大模型to b的颠覆与边界 enterprise software saas pricing ai for b2b fde sap organizational inertia pricing, not code, is where ai actually hits sap ai's impact on sap is not at the code layer but on the business model. sap's share price has come back down from a high of $300 to $160, but stretched back to 2021 it is still up more than 20%; adobe has fallen from around 480 to roughly 220, and zoom has fallen to almost nothing. what actually gets replaced is single-point saas. the core of the impact is the traditional per-seat pricing model, which will shift toward charging by consumption and even by outcome — a challenge every enterprise software company has to face. yuan xin sap won't train a foundation model; it partners openly instead sap does not train a general-purpose large model of its own, because foundation models are evolving too fast, and because what sap is good at is enterprise process, data and interaction. its approach is to stay open to all third-party models and, on model selection, to fit the most suitable model to the most suitable scenario. in parallel, it trains proprietary small models on its own structured table data — rpt 1.5 — for finance scenarios such as collections forecasting, where the accuracy requirement is close to 100%, because in finance 99% accuracy is still unusable. yuan xin the boss wants ai, but the dirty data is still there the biggest headache for cios at large enterprises is the boss reading some article on wechat and tossing it over with ‘i want that too’. the gap is that everyone assumes that now ai has arrived, the dirty, grinding work no longer has to be done. ai can speed up data cleaning, but it cannot make that process disappear. getting ai to land still requires fdes to comb through historical data and organize it by business object, and at the same time to distill the unstructured judgment of the veteran hands, settling it into enterprise memory — only then does the share of work that can be executed automatically gradually rise. yuan xin fdes and erp consultants will merge into one hybrid role the fde is not a relabeled on-site engineer. a traditional erp consultant is an industry expert who enters from the business side and ultimately lands requirements inside a standard product; an fde is a product builder deployed to the customer early, and the capability that accumulates flows back into the product. early fdes leaned toward low-level engineering and lacked a translator to turn business into coding requirements, which is why anthropic and openai have started working with consulting firms like mckinsey and accenture. the two groups will merge into a composite role that understands business and technology at once — exactly the route that spillover from a small circle into the enterprise market has to take. yuan xin customs agent accuracy flipped once old process assets were reused one large innovative company built its own agent to handle customs declarations for 33 countries and got only 60-70% accuracy; h: no one confirmed the doors were shut: institutional carelessness was the real killer in 1987 the roll-on/roll-off ferry herald of free enterprise capsized with her bow doors open, killing 193 people. the real culprit was not the sleeping crewman but a system that left everyone feeling this was not their job. the most valuable thing here is the demonstration of how a company culture in which nobody made a mistake managed to kill 193 people. for anyone who writes processes, assigns responsibilities or runs safety audits, it cuts deeper than any textbook on institutional design. operations and safety leads in high-risk industries, plus founders and managers who have to design error-proof processes for their teams. cautionary tales with tim harford cautionary tales the doors of death: the herald of free enterprise maritime disaster organizational failure safety culture accountability regulatory lag swiss cheese model closing the bow doors was one man's job, and he was asleep a roll-on/roll-off ferry is designed so that vehicles drive straight into the hold, with a large door at the bow and another at the stern that must be closed before sailing. closing them was the job of assistant boatswain mark stanley. on a cold evening in march 1987, his superior told him to go below and rest, and to come back on duty when the announcement came. he made a cup of tea, sat down on his bunk and dozed off. four years earlier, another roll-on/roll-off ship belonging to the same company had put to sea with its doors open because the man responsible for closing them had fallen asleep; that time, nothing happened. tim harford captains asked for a door indicator light and executives turned them down after the sister ship sailed twice with her doors open, one captain wrote a memo telling the crew to take the matter seriously. another pointed out that the bridge had no way of seeing the state of the doors and proposed fitting indicator lights. senior management's response was that the man closing the doors could be assumed to tell the bridge if something went wrong; one asked whether they should also fit an indicator light to show whether the storekeeper was awake. nobody took the proposal forward. the captains had spotted the gap in advance, and no one was willing to close it. tim harford the ship went over in a minute and a half and 193 people died the herald of free enterprise left port carrying 459 passengers and 80 crew, and seawater poured through the open doors onto the vehicle deck. passengers first joked about the spilled meal trays; then the ship rolled over as though something had been pulled out from underneath her, and within a minute and a half she was lying on her side on a sandbank. inside it was pitch black and freezing, and life jackets tangled people up rather than saving them. some escaped by stepping on other people's faces; others arched their backs to make human bridges so that strangers and children could climb across. in the end 193 people died. tim harford four links in the chain each looked innocent on their own justice sheen found that the disaster was not the work of one man. stanley had fallen asleep. his superior said that closing the doors had never been his job. under company policy, the first officer only had to confirm that the man responsible was near the doors. and under another policy, the captain assumed that no report meant everything was fine. none of these four things was gravely wrong on its own; put together, they left every line of defence wide open. james reason later distilled the swiss cheese model from this accident: disaster happens when the holes in successive layers of defence line up exactly. tim harford the judge pointed the finger at the top of the company sheen's conclusion was unambiguous: "the fundamental fault lay at a higher level in the company." the board of townsend thoresen had never treated safety as its own responsibility. overloading went unchecked; the company did not know how many people were actually on board. the bow and stern draught figures were invented by the crew, because nobody ever checked them. in sheen's own words, "the body corporate was infected with the disease of sloppiness." but the court of inquiry had no power to punish, and although the coroner's jury returned a verdict of unlawful killing, it could not name a single individual either. tim harford the law could not keep up with the new technology the roro ferry was an innovation, but maritime law had been written before it existed. the law only prohibited leaving an unseaworthy ship in port; h: a 28nm chip outruns the leading edge by 1,000x: compute-in-memory black magic without euv zhicun technology (知存科技) turned 28nm flash into compute-in-memory chips. because the physics make larger arrays more energy-efficient, efficiency rises as models get bigger — and transformers are pure upside for the approach. a rare episode that takes the physics of compute-in-memory, the process choice behind it, and four years of tape-out failures all the way down, with unusual candour from the founder. engineers who care about the underlying architecture of ai chips, semiconductor investors, and founders who want to understand what the compute bottleneck actually is. 老石谈芯 老石谈芯 28纳米反超1000倍?不需要euv的芯片黑魔法：对话知存科技王绍迪 compute-in-memory ai chips memory transformer semiconductor manufacturing on-device ai no chip company had heard of compute-in-memory, so founding one was the only route wang shaodi (王绍迪) already wanted to build compute-in-memory chips while he was doing his phd. before graduating in 2016 he approached four or five leading chip companies in china and the us; none of them had heard of the technology, and none was going to open up a new direction for a freshly minted phd. academia was no better — a professor at peking university asked him outright where the funding was supposed to come from, and at the time very few chip projects anywhere in china had budgets above a million yuan, not even enough to pay for a tape-out. with both routes closed, the only option left was to start a company himself. wang shaodi the bigger the model, the faster the read — the exact reverse of von neumann in a conventional von neumann architecture, doing a matrix multiplication means reading the data out of the memory cells one by one and shipping it to the compute unit; the bigger the memory array, the slower that read becomes, and that is dictated by physics. compute-in-memory instead turns each memory cell itself into one compute node inside the matrix multiplication: a single activation completes the computation for an entire matrix, with no reading row by row and column by column. that means an algorithm that grows from a few rows to ten thousand rows still needs only one activation, so effective bandwidth and effective compute go up as the model gets bigger — precisely the opposite of how the von neumann architecture behaves. wang shaodi the black magic is just ohm's law: voltage times conductance equals current the core of compute-in-memory is using the physical relationship in ohm's law — voltage times conductance equals current — to perform multiplication directly. you apply a voltage along the row direction of the memory; each memory cell is itself a conductance value; and the current that naturally flows out along the column direction is the product of voltage and conductance. within a single column, the currents from multiple rows converge, which physically performs the addition. the whole matrix multiplication is finished inside one read, with no need for the adder and multiplier circuits of a digital chip at all. in essence, it uses the most basic electrical relationship from middle-school physics to do ai computation. wang shaodi the most ordinary memory won because flash draws the least compute current faced with a range of storage media — sram, non-volatile flash, the rram that academia was excited about — zhicun picked the one that looked least remarkable: nor flash. the reason is that the compute current flash needs to do analog multiplication is the lowest of any memory, and in compute-in-memory the more cells you can switch on simultaneously, the larger the scale you can process in parallel; lower current therefore means a larger array can be turned on and stronger effective compute. flash is also the most mature memory process, which makes tape-out and debugging fastest. the price was the fight over precision: it took several hundred people at the company seven to eight years to get accuracy to the point where it met application requirements. wang shaodi transformers are pure upside for compute-in-memory, not a new problem the shift from deep learning to transformers handed compute-in-memory two dividends. first, deep learning would often read a parameter once and then compute with it tens of thousands of times, so memory bandwidth was not under much pressure; a transformer reads each parameter once and computes with it once, giving a read-to-compute ratio that is 1 to 1 by nature, whereas architectures like gpus are typically 64 to 1 or 128 to 1, and the bad cases reach 1,000 to 1. that is a perfect match for compute-in-memory, whose memory-to-compute ratio is also 1 to 1. second, the matrices in a transformer are 1,000 to 10,000 times larger than in deep learning, and since compute-in-memory finishes an entire matrix in one go, a larger matrix lifts computational efficiency by that same 1,000 to 10,000 times. on top of that, large models only need int4, that is 4-bit precision, far below the 12 to 16 bits the

fiat is running first because consumer protection is mature, while stablecoins are still working on irreversibility. real cases — a 200 hong kong dollar spending cap, a token that burned through more than us$600 — plus a protocol map covering stripe, visa, openai and google. denser than most ai narratives. founders building ai applications, payments, or cross-border e-commerce; product managers watching agent commercialization; investors trying to judge where payment infrastructure is heading. what's next｜科技早知道 科技早知道 可以给你的 agent 发一点零花钱了 | s10e22 ai agent agent payments payment protocols visa stablecoins agent payments split into two scenarios, and only one is genuinely new gao ning (高宁) and patrick break agent payment into two categories. in the first, the user has an explicit need — e-commerce shopping, booking a service — and the agent simply executes it; the end consumer is still a human. in the second, the agent generates spending on its own while carrying out a task: calling an api, buying a research report, downloading materials. the amounts are small but the frequency is high, and it has to happen autonomously within an authorized limit. the first category is larger in volume with a longer chain; the second is the net-new scenario, and today it mostly happens inside a user's conversation with a closed-source model such as openai or claude. gao ning the blocker is not the technology: trust, card custody, and merchant readiness patrick argues the biggest problem right now sits in three places, none of them technical. first, the agent's intelligence and recommendation quality have not yet earned user trust — having your context does not mean it knows what you like. second, the agent cannot be trusted to hold your card details; if a chargeback happens, the user bears the responsibility. third, merchants have doubts about who owns the customer relationship when an agent places the order, and with agent penetration among ordinary users still low, the roi on a large merchant-side investment does not add up. that is why merchant readiness is moving slowly. patrick clink ran vic's first transaction by making the accountability chain explicit patrick describes the partnership with visa: clink is positioned as the first agent enableer inside visa's global production network. at the end of june, at an expo, it executed vic's first transaction. the flow works like this: the agent passes the user's context, the authorized limit and the product category to clink, which records it as a mandate; once the agent has found the item, clink checks it against the original authorization, then requests a one-time payment capability from visa, and visa verifies and completes the payment. the mechanism makes the final chain of accountability clear. patrick fiat is ahead of stablecoins because consumer protection makes trust solvable patrick explains why clink chose fiat over stablecoins. in the fiat system, consumer protection mechanisms are mature: banks and card networks have complete processes for authorization and dispute handling, which makes the trust problem far easier to solve. with stablecoins, once a payment goes out it is essentially irreversible, and both consumer confidence and sustained trust take the damage. a guest then adds a real case: after one company fired an employee, a token burned through more than us$600 overnight with no way to trace it. they ended up giving each person a separate api key so spending could be traced. patrick stablecoins are building an on-chain alipay; the rails exist, the scenarios don't gao ning walks through progress in the stablecoin lane. plain small-value transfers are already fairly mature, because an on-chain payment is simply an end-to-end transfer. the more interesting work is people trying to solve the problem taobao faced in its early days: users and merchants do not trust each other. the approach is to use a smart contract to lock the money in a neutral position and release it to the merchant only after delivery is confirmed — solving the irreversibility of "i paid and nothing shipped." gao ning's view is that the infrastructure for small, high-frequency payments is no longer what's missing; what's missing is a richer set of scenarios and a shift in user habits. gao ning clink is not building a new highway, it is building the ramps between them patrick says clink is not laying down another highway; h: embodied ai hasn't reached its gpt-1 moment; the block is data that won't scale shen yujun (沈宇军) of ant lingbo (蚂蚁灵波) argues embodied ai has not reached its gpt-1 moment, and the bottleneck is that data has not scaled up: internet data is two orders of magnitude larger than real-robot data, and an ideal pretraining run would start at a million hours. to get there the team rebuilt visual pretraining from scratch and insists on starting from real sensors. it is a rare episode that works all the way through the engineering trade-offs of a natively embodied model and the real data bottleneck, and it is honest about what moe and unidirectional modeling cost to train. useful if you are trying to judge when embodied ai hits its inflection point. embodied-ai founders, robotics algorithm engineers, and investors following ai in the physical world — especially teams still torn between building the brain and building the body. 张小珺·商业访谈录 张小珺·商业访谈录 147. 和蚂蚁灵波沈宇军聊：机器人原生基础模型、大脑和本体的关系、预训练与数据scale up、老师汤晓鸥 embodied ai robot brains pretraining data ant lingbo founding a startup giving up on gan: it uses too little of the compute you give it shen yujun has worked on generative models since 2017, and his team kept pushing on scaling gans — even after diffusion took off, they made one last attempt earlier this year. it was better than their work of previous years, but the fundamental problem with gan is how little of the available compute it can actually put to use: diffusion can iterate many times to produce a single image, while gan runs out of capacity when the content gets complex, video especially. they open-sourced what they had accumulated on gan and closed the chapter, though he thinks the know-how from adversarial training — running two models at once, playing them off against each other — will not go to waste. shen yujun digital-world models do not fit the physical world's requirements the first-generation model relied on a digital-world model for pretraining, but the team found that the motivations driving digital-world development do not match what the physical world needs: video generation chases image quality, and robot actions simply do not require high image quality. the digital world moves on its own iteration cycle, and there was no way to push back upstream and get the model changed for them. so in 2026 they decided to rebuild everything around physical-world requirements: everything vision-related, both understanding and generation, is trained from scratch, and only the language model continues to reuse an llm. their other commitment is to start from real sensors, precisely because real sensors are noisy — which is inherently at odds with the clean datasets academia works on. shen yujun depth estimation had to be relearned from geometry, not semantics the first-generation depth model used dino v2, a digital-world semantic model, and semantic understanding is not enough for the physical world — knowing there is a dog there is not the same as knowing how far away it is. this time they dropped dino and redid pretraining entirely from a geometric angle — points, lines, surfaces, edges — then iterated a new depth estimation model on top. two examples: on a reflective faucet, the new model can see where the water flow is; and a cat behind a glass door is completely invisible to the new depth model, because the cat is blocked by the glass and only gradually appears once you pull the door open. in semantic understanding the cat is there the whole time; in spatial perception you have to hit the door first. that is why semantic pretraining from the digital world does not transfer directly to the physical world. shen yujun native to the physical world means unidirectional modeling and moe generating video in the digital world can afford to wait 30 seconds, so bidirectional attention is available; robot execution has to be real time, and history cannot see the future, so the model has to be unidirectional. that cost them three to four months of training unidirectional attention from scratch — forcing a bidirectional model into a unidirectional one causes the pretrained knowledge to be forgotten, so that route had to be abandoned. the other technical piece is native moe: every expert has to be activated with equal probability, because sparsity only counts as real sparsity if it is evenly spread, and just getting moe to work took two months and dozens of failures. the physical world lets you sacrifice image quality, and that is where the room for efficiency optimization comes from. shen yujun the gpt-1 moment has not arrived, and data is what is blocking it shen yujun's judgment is that embodied ai has not reached its gpt-1 moment today, because no good way to scale up data has emerged yet. this time they used 60,000 hours of real-robot data, but that is not an order-of-magnitude increase, and it is nowhere near enough. h: yao song: physical ai is won by systems, not by young geniuses from deephi to orienspace to striding ai, yao song (姚颂) argues that what decides physical ai is not one or two genius algorithms but data, compute, a talent pool and commercial delivery at every milestone — and that the intelligence-first giants may not be the ones who get to pick the fruit. the episode runs two hours and fifty-five minutes and the density stays high. yao song uses three companies to work all the way through funding trade-offs, how to prioritise in commercial spaceflight, and the split over which road physical ai should take. he makes concrete calls, not slogans. founders and investors preparing to move into embodied intelligence; anyone trying to understand the funding logic and cycles of chinese hard tech; yao song's early years are also a useful reference for engineers thinking about a switch. 晚点聊 latetalk 晚点聊 173: 对话姚颂：深鉴、东方空间、再出发，「天才少年」十年后 physical ai embodied intelligence commercial spaceflight startup playbook tsinghua network ai chips offered boring or suffering, yao song keeps choosing suffering yao song remembers entering tsinghua's electronic engineering department in 2011 and setting himself a rule: eleven hours of study every day, with the clock paused for toilet breaks and meals. he admits there were simply too many people at tsinghua who were ‘both smart and hardworking’, and diligence was the only way he could buy himself any sense of safety. not until the second semester of his freshman year did he realise that university did not have to follow a single track. a teacher later summed it up for him: life is either boring or suffering. yao song took the second — he cannot stand the placid life of a silicon valley engineer, and that fear of boredom is what keeps pushing him back into hard-tech startups. song yao taking all three chip giants' money would have made deephi unsellable deephi (深鉴科技) met 50 institutions before its angel round and was turned down by all of them; in the end zhang yutong (张予彤) and lin renjun (林仁俊) at gsr ventures (金沙江创投) understood the direction and invested. what he is proudest of is a strategic choice in fundraising: bringing xilinx into the a round while turning down nvidia and intel. his reasoning ran like this — if the endgame is an ipo or an acquisition, having all three chip giants on the cap table is actually dangerous. they compete with each other, so none of them would genuinely open up business resources, and at acquisition time they could bid the price up and make trouble until the company could not be sold at all. so he picked one: xilinx, a direct competitor of nvidia that also badly needed software capability. song yao the darkest stretch came after the exit, not after any failure in 2018 xilinx acquired deephi for more than us$3 billion. yao song says he paced happily around the table for two minutes after signing the contract, and then his life went dark. up to that point the direction had been set by his advisor wang yu (汪玉); this was the first time he had to decide his own next step, and there was no road ahead of him, only fog. at 26 he describes himself as being in something like a midlife crisis — he did not even want to scroll his phone, nothing held his interest. that loss of a sense of purpose tormented him more than failure would have, and it became the starting point for taking a part-time role at matrix partners china and searching for a direction systematically. song yao what zhang ying gave him was information, not cash to find a new direction, yao song became a part-time venture partner at matrix partners china (经纬创投) at the end of 2018. zhang ying (张颖) told him: you don't need cash, what you need is information. every partners' meeting and every investment committee meeting was open to him. he swept systematically through lidar, brain-computer interfaces, gpus and controlled fusion: li yifan (李一凡) convinced him that the moat in lidar is engineering capability rather than the technical route; brain-computer interfaces in china have to pass through too long an approval cycle; gpus were blocked by the non-compete terms attached to the acquisition; fusion is too far from industrialisation. in the end he waited until the commercial-space window opened. song yao reliability, payload, speed, then cost — the order cannot be reversed yao song breaks chinese commercial spaceflight into three words — china, commercial, spaceflight — and then ranks the priorities: good, many, fast, cheap. good means a high success rate; h: open weights now trail closed models by 3-5 months, and that lag is the whole safety margin kimi k3 compresses the open-versus-closed gap from the 6-9 months people had been arguing over down to 3-5 months, and that lag is the only risk buffer anyone has — heavy-handed regulation of open weights would merely postpone the inevitable while voiding the buffer itself. this is a judgment piece that reads k3 as an inflection point for the whole ecosystem: the decelerationist economics of open weights, where chinese labs' capital efficiency comes from, and the asymmetry in us policy — three arguments you can use directly. it is not a model review. investors tracking the us-china model landscape, engineering leads who have to choose between open weights and closed apis, and anyone doing analysis on ai export controls and open-source policy. interconnects interconnects kimi k3: the open-weights escalation open weights us-china competition capital efficiency moe architecture ai policy the frontier gap has been compressed to three to five months k3 is a 2.8t-parameter moe, released july 16 with the weights promised for july 27. the author pins the entire piece's key conclusion on a single number: the performance gap between open and closed models — or between the us and china — has narrowed from the 6-9 months people had been arguing over to 3-5 months. he adds a robustness note: even if moonshot never delivers the open weights, as long as china has a closed model of equivalent strength, most of the inferences only land somewhere in the middle, and the direction is unchanged. the leaderboard evidence: second overall on vals ai, third on the artificial analysis intelligence index (losing only to claude fable and gpt-5.6 sol max, and cheaper than both), first on frontend code arena. this is the closest an open model has come to the frontier since deepseek r1. nathan lambert distillation explains almost none of what k3 achieved the author states the conclusion outright: if adversarial distillation contributed to k3 at all, it did so only to a very small degree. his reasoning is that r1 and k3 are different in kind — r1 was a chinese lab pivoting to reasoning models extremely fast and getting there first, while k3 is scaling along already-known directions in data, algorithms, architecture, tooling and environments, which is to say the same set of problems people at openai and anthropic are working on right now. a second line of evidence comes from his trip to china: kimi's team culture was one of the few he could feel immediately among the companies he visited, with strong individual execution and freedom of expression despite gpu constraints. having met them, the result did not surprise him. he expects the distillation argument and the pressure around it to continue, but says observers who attribute chinese models to ip theft will be proven wrong by reality. nathan lambert the waic speech is beijing declaring its tolerance for open-weight risk until now there had been almost no national-level chinese policy statement on open-source ai — as far as the author knows, no senior official had commented publicly. that changed this week: in his keynote at the world artificial intelligence conference (waic), xi jinping (习近平) very directly staked the future of china's ai ecosystem on open source and global diffusion. the author reads it this way: that commitment landing in the same week as the strongest open-weight model in history amounts to an implicit statement of china's risk tolerance for open weights. the simplest explanation is that the chinese government is tracking model risk closely, possibly at a finer technical granularity than america's "vibes-based regulation," and would act if it measured real risk — and it currently judges that frontier models pose no substantive risk. at the same time, economic policymakers think getting ai adopted first is good: build distribution, monetize later, the same path as cars, solar and advanced manufacturing. nathan lambert open weights are decelerationist because they cut frontier labs' margins dean ball — personally a supporter of open source, though now at openai — says open-weight models are fundamentally decelerationist, and the author says he is right. the transmission chain is concrete: strong open models sharply compress the gross-margin room of closed labs, which means both less profit to reinvest in the next generation of models and a market markdown of these companies' terminal values, which in turn discounts future funding rounds. together, those push back the arrival of the most transformative models. but the author does not think this is enough to knock openai and anthropic out of the ranks of the world's most valuable companies, and he thinks it is net good for society: on the diffusion side open weights are accelerationist, driving down the entry price of intelligence at a given performance tier and encouraging h: why cross-entropy loss won: it is training a text compressor cross-entropy loss was selected because it can be proved mathematically to be the only functional form that guarantees the loss is minimized exactly when the model's output equals the true distribution of the data — and that turns out to be equivalent to training the model into a text compressor approaching the shannon limit. it nails two frames that sound entirely unrelated — next-token prediction and compression — together with a single formula. for people who want to understand why the loss function has the shape it has, not just how to call it. engineers and researchers interested in loss function design and in the intersection of information theory and deep learning, especially anyone who wants to understand where the name cross-entropy loss comes from. andrej karpathy andrej karpathy but what is cross-entropy? | compression is intelligence part 2 information theory cross-entropy language model training distillation compression kl divergence gzip alone can draw a family tree of human languages a 2002 paper used nothing but gzip — an ordinary general-purpose file compressor — to cluster texts in different languages automatically, and even to recover the genealogical tree of the language families, without relying on any linguistic prior knowledge at any point. the method is to append a fragment of document b to the end of document a, compress the result, and compare its file size against compressing a on its own. that difference is essentially asking how well a compression scheme optimized for a handles a fragment of b. the same idea was later used for authorship identification. grant sanderson an old code meeting a new distribution wastes bits: that is cross-entropy suppose a coding scheme is optimized for some distribution q — say the robot commands up/down/left/right are assigned probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8 and given bit lengths to match — but the actual data has shifted to a new distribution p. keeping the old code now wastes bits. reweight that old code by the new distribution and compute the average number of bits it consumes: that value is the cross-entropy of q relative to p. what it measures is exactly this — how a compression scheme optimized for one situation performs when moved into another. grant sanderson cross-entropy bottoms out at the entropy itself, exactly when q equals p picture the cross-entropy formula as a curve: hold p fixed and let q vary. the curve always attains its minimum where q equals p, and that minimum is precisely the entropy of p. the reason is that the question cross-entropy asks — how does a code optimized for one setting perform in another — can only reach the theoretical optimum in compression efficiency when the two settings are exactly the same. this property is the hinge on which the whole subsequent argument turns. grant sanderson pretraining loss is nothing but the average information content per token when you train a language model, for every real next token in the training data you take the negative logarithm of the probability the model assigned to it, then average over all tokens. that is the entire pretraining loss function. the smarter the model, the higher the probability it puts on the token that actually occurred, and the lower the corresponding negative log — the information content, the degree of surprise. a badly trained model, by contrast, is confident about nothing and is startled everywhere. grant sanderson the negative log is forced out by mathematics, not chosen by you the common explanation is that in the cross-entropy formula every term other than the one for the true token is zero, so what remains is naturally the negative log — but that does not explain why you reached for cross-entropy in the first place. the sturdier argument is this: require only that some function f satisfy the condition that the average loss over all training examples attains its minimum only when the model's output distribution equals the true statistical distribution of the data. constrained optimization with lagrange multipliers then proves that f must be the logarithm. the choice was never yours; the negative log is forced out by the mathematics — and the average-loss formula you arrive at is exactly the definition of cross-entropy. grant sanderson distillation feeds the small model the large model's entire probability distribution ordinary pretraining puts full weight on exactly one token per position — the one that actually occurred — and zero on everything else. distillation instead has the small model match, at every position, the complete probability distribution the large model produces, with the loss defined as the cross-entropy of the small model's distribution relative to the large model's. a single training example therefore transmits far more information than it does in ordinary pretraining — like learning chess not by watching
